items.title: Transform Stage
items.text:
Changes the attributes of log records, metric data points and spans, and of their scopes and resources, with the statements of the driver chosen by driver. The driver's options are under the driver's name, e.g. cel:. Use it to derive attributes from others, rename keys to a convention, cut long values, or remove attributes nobody should store. To look values up in a table, use the Value Map Stage instead; to encrypt or hash values, the Encryption Stage.

Type: transform

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description driver string Yes - The language of the statements: cel (Common Expression Language) on_error string No skip What happens when a statement fails on a resource, scope or entry: skip the statement and keep the entry, drop the entry (or the resource or scope with its entries), or reject the event (422 for OTLP clients) cel object With driver: cel - Options of the CEL driver, see below

CEL driver options: a list of statements per signal, at least one list.

Field Type Description logs []statement Statements for logs metrics []statement Statements for metrics, applied to their data points traces []statement Statements for traces

Statements: each has exactly one operation, which names the target path, and an optional when:

Operation Arguments Effect set value: CEL expression Sets the attribute to the value: a string, bool, int, double or bytes. Replaces an existing value delete - Removes the attribute; a missing one is no error rename to: key Moves the value to the key to in the same attributes, replacing a value there; a missing attribute is no error truncate length: int ≥ 1 Shortens a string value to length characters; other types stay as they are (any) when: CEL expression The statement only runs where it returns true

Target paths and when statements run: the path decides how often a statement runs, so a statement on the resource runs once per resource, not once per record that shares it:

Path Runs once per CEL variables resource.attributes['key'] resource resource scope.attributes['key'] scope resource, scope attributes['key'] log record, metric data point or span resource, scope, and record (logs), metric and datapoint (metrics) or span (traces) 
flowchart LR
    event(["event, copied"]) --> resource["resource statements<br/>once per resource"]
    resource --> scope["scope statements<br/>once per scope"]
    scope --> entry["entry statements<br/>once per record, data point or span"]
    entry --> next(["next stage or sink"])
    resource -. "failed statement" .-> onerror{"on_error"}
    scope -.-> onerror
    entry -.-> onerror
    onerror -- skip --> continue["next statement"]
    onerror -- drop --> dropped["entry, scope or resource removed"]
    onerror -- reject --> rejected["event rejected, 422"]

Within a signal, the resource statements run first, then the scope statements, then the entry statements, each group in the order of the list. Keys go in single or double quotes.

Functions: besides standard CEL, expressions have the string functions of CEL, e.g. split, replace, lowerAscii, substring, trim, and attr(attributes, 'key'), which returns the value of an attribute: a string, bool, int, double or bytes, or null if it is missing. Arrays and key-value lists are returned as their OTLP AnyValue.

Example: derive the environment from the namespace, drop a secret, follow the semantic conventions and keep notes short:

{
  "name": "normalize",
  "type": "transform",
  "from": "otlp-in",
  "spec": {
    "driver": "cel",
    "cel": {
      "logs": [
        {
          "set": "resource.attributes['deployment.environment']",
          "value": "attr(resource.attributes, 'k8s.namespace.name').split('-')[1]"
        },
        { "delete": "attributes['password']" },
        { "rename": "attributes['user']", "to": "user.name" },
        { "truncate": "attributes['note']", "length": 256 },
        {
          "set": "attributes['level']",
          "value": "record.severity_text.lowerAscii()",
          "when": "record.severity_text != ''"
        }
      ],
      "metrics": [
        { "rename": "attributes['http.method']", "to": "http.request.method" }
      ]
    }
  }
}

examples/tests/otlp_with_transform.json holds this stream with test cases; run them with tram test.

Metrics: besides the node metrics of its stream, the stage counts the statements that failed, with the stream, the node of the stage and the signal as labels:

Metric Type Labels Description tram_stage_transform_failed_total Counter stream, node, signal Statements that failed on a resource, scope or entry, whatever on_error then did

The node metrics framework counts records and durations only, not failed statements, which is why the stage adds its own counter, created from the meter provider its factory passes. It is labeled like the node metrics, so every stream and stage has a series of its own. The first failure in a minute is also logged as a warning with its error.

Behavior
  • The stage changes a copy of the signals it has statements for; the event it receives is shared with sibling branches and stays as it is. Signals without statements are passed on as they are
  • A statement fails when an expression fails, e.g. on a missing attribute (null has no split), or returns a value that is no string, bool, int, double or bytes. With on_error: skip, use when or attr(...) != null to run a statement only where it applies, so the failed metric shows real problems
  • A resource or scope that an event does not have is created for statements that set something on it, and left out again otherwise
  • With drop, scopes and resources that lose all their entries are removed, and an event that loses all of them is not passed on
  • The statements are compiled when the stream is created or updated, so an invalid statement fails the request, also as a dry run, naming the statement and its signal
  • Each entry statement costs a CEL evaluation per log record, data point or span; resource and scope statements run once per resource and scope and cost little; prefer resource statements where the value is the same for all entries of a resource
  • The stage holds no events back and does not count toward the Hold Times

items.title: Performance
items.text:
Entry statements are evaluated once per log record, data point or span, and every additional one adds its evaluation, while scope and resource statements are evaluated once per scope and resource. The rows are measured on the shapes of the Value Map Stage benchmark, so the two stages compare.

Component Per record CPU per record Allocs per record Records/s Spread transform (CEL), one entry statement 622.7 ns 1.03 µs 13.1 1.61 M ±9% transform (CEL), four entry statements of a normalization 850.6 ns 1.40 µs 18.1 1.18 M ±22% ⚠️ transform (CEL), one resource statement 88.9 ns 230.0 ns 3.2 11.25 M ±7%

Measured on 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-13700K, commit 79dd4fb, 2026-11-23; compare with other components under Where the Time Goes.

items.title: Validation Stage
items.text:
Checks each incoming event as a whole — one OTLP request, one broker message, or one batch — against the rules of the driver chosen by driver, and passes it on, drops it, or rejects it. The driver's options are under the driver's name, e.g. cel:. To keep only matching records, use the Filter Stage.

Type: validation

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description driver string Yes - The technology of the rules: cel (Common Expression Language) on_mismatch string Yes - Action when a signal does not match its rule: "drop" or "reject" cel object With driver: cel - Options of the CEL driver, see below

CEL driver options:

Field Type Required Default Description logs string No - CEL expression evaluated once for all logs of an event. Must return a boolean. Without it, all logs match metrics string No - CEL expression evaluated once for all metrics of an event. Must return a boolean. Without it, all metrics match traces string No - CEL expression evaluated once for all traces of an event. Must return a boolean. Without it, all traces match

CEL Expression Context: - Each expression receives the complete payload of its signal type: logs (LogsData), metrics (MetricsData), or traces (TracesData) - An event can contain several signal types, e.g. after a batch stage. Each type present is checked with its own expression - Use the full protobuf structure, e.g. logs.resource_logs.all(...), and write the expression as a condition that every accepted delivery has to fulfil

On Mismatch Behavior: - drop - Removes all data of the signal type that did not match. Other signal types of the event are still passed on; if nothing is left, nothing is passed on - reject - Rejects the whole event with an error. The OTLP source answers with HTTP 422, the Broker Source rejects the message instead of redelivering it

Example: reject log deliveries in which a resource has no service.name:

{
  "name": "require-service-name",
  "type": "validation",
  "from": "source",
  "spec": {
    "driver": "cel",
    "on_mismatch": "reject",
    "cel": {
      "logs": "logs.resource_logs.all(r, r.resource.attributes.exists(a, a.key == 'service.name'))"
    }
  }
}

Additional Examples:

Drop metric deliveries that contain a metric without a name: 

{
  "driver": "cel",
  "on_mismatch": "drop",
  "cel": {
    "metrics": "metrics.resource_metrics.all(r, r.scope_metrics.all(s, s.metrics.all(m, m.name != '')))"
  }
}

Reject trace deliveries that contain a span without a valid trace ID: 

{
  "driver": "cel",
  "on_mismatch": "reject",
  "cel": {
    "traces": "traces.resource_spans.all(r, r.scope_spans.all(s, s.spans.all(span, size(span.trace_id) == 16)))"
  }
}

Reject log deliveries that contain a record whose tenant.id is not a lowercase UUID. matches takes an RE2 regular expression and finds it anywhere in the value, so anchor it with ^ and $. Checking a value that a Broker Sink puts into its NATS subjects keeps out dots, whitespace and wildcards, which would make the subject invalid or change its meaning: 

{
  "driver": "cel",
  "on_mismatch": "reject",
  "cel": {
    "logs": "logs.resource_logs.all(r, r.scope_logs.all(s, s.log_records.all(record, record.attributes.exists(a, a.key == 'tenant.id' && a.value.string_value.matches('^[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}$')))))"
  }
}

Behavior
  • The decision applies to the whole event. An expression like log_records.exists(record, record.severity_text == 'ERROR') passes on a delivery with one ERROR and many INFO records in full, including the INFO records
  • A rule that fails for an event, e.g. a CEL expression accessing a missing list index, rejects the whole event regardless of on_mismatch. The OTLP source answers with HTTP 422, the Broker Source rejects the message instead of redelivering it
  • Place validation stages with on_mismatch: reject before a batch stage, so one invalid delivery does not reject the deliveries batched with it

items.title: Performance
items.text:
An expression that only looks at resources is far cheaper than one that walks every record, since there are far fewer resources than records; prefer resource-level rules where they suffice.

Component Per record CPU per record Allocs per record Records/s Spread validation (CEL), record-level expression 1.14 µs 1.38 µs 9.1 873 k ±3% validation (CEL), resource-level expression 13.5 ns 16.1 ns 0.1 74.24 M ±41% ⚠️

Measured on 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-13700K, commit 79dd4fb, 2026-11-23; compare with other components under Where the Time Goes.

items.title: Value Map Stage
items.text:
Looks up a source attribute in a table for every record and sets a target attribute to the mapped value, or to default on a miss (missing attribute or no table entry). Every record is passed on; nothing is filtered, dropped or held back. It maps values by data, a table; to compute attributes from others by logic, use the Transform Stage, e.g. after this stage on its result.

Type: value_map

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description source_attr string Yes - Attribute whose value is looked up target_attr string Yes - Attribute set to the result of the lookup. An existing attribute of that name is replaced default string Yes - Value set when the source attribute is missing or its value has no table entry level string No "record" Level the source attribute is read from: record (the record's own attributes) or resource (the attributes of the record's resource) table object One of table, table_ref - Embedded lookup table, source value to target value. In a Kubernetes Stream resource, the table can come from config maps selected by label, which keeps large tables out of the resource; see Config Maps table_ref string One of table, table_ref - Path to a JSON file that holds the lookup table as an object of string values, e.g. {"value-a": "target-a"}. Read once when the stage is created; an unreadable file or invalid JSON is rejected. Exactly one of table and table_ref has to be set

The target attribute is always set on the record itself, whatever level the source attribute is read from. A source value that is not a string cannot have a table entry and receives the default value.

Example: translate a team attribute into a team.id attribute:

{
  "name": "team-ids",
  "type": "value_map",
  "from": "otlp-in",
  "spec": {
    "source_attr": "team",
    "target_attr": "team.id",
    "default": "unassigned",
    "table": {
      "team-0": "cart",
      "team-1": "checkout"
    }
  }
}

Metrics: besides the node metrics of its stream, the stage records its lookup outcomes, with the stream, the node of the stage and the signal as labels:

Metric Type Labels Description tram_stage_value_map_mapped_total Counter stream, node, signal Records whose source value the table maps, which received the mapped value tram_stage_value_map_lookup_missing_attr_total Counter stream, node, signal Records without the source attribute, which received the default value tram_stage_value_map_lookup_no_entry_total Counter stream, node, signal Records whose source value has no table entry, which received the default value

The node metrics framework counts records and durations only, not lookup outcomes, which is why the stage adds its own counters, created from the meter provider its factory passes. They are labeled like the node metrics, so every stream and stage has a series of its own.

Behavior
  • A lookup miss is a defined state, not an error: the record is still passed on, with the target attribute set to default
  • Every record is annotated, so the stage always passes on a copy of the event: the containers it annotates (records of each signal) are rebuilt, resources, scopes and metric metadata are shared
  • The table is fixed while the stream runs. To change it, update the stream with a changed spec, through the API, the config sync or a Stream resource, or change the config maps a Stream resource selects its table from; the usual stream update applies: an update with an identical spec changes nothing, an update with just a changed spec replaces the stage without touching the source
  • The stage holds no events back and does not count toward the Hold Times

items.title: Performance
items.text:
Mapping a resource attribute runs once per resource instead of once per record, so it is cheaper where the source attribute lives on the resource.

Component Per record CPU per record Allocs per record Records/s Spread value_map, mapping a record attribute 122.8 ns 296.8 ns 5.0 8.15 M ±1% value_map, mapping a resource attribute 127.8 ns 310.8 ns 5.0 7.82 M ±5%

Measured on 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-13700K, commit 79dd4fb, 2026-11-23; compare with other components under Where the Time Goes.

items.title: Container Image
items.text:
Every release publishes a multi-architecture image (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) as ghcr.io/go-tram/tram:<version>, e.g. 0.0.19, and as latest. It is signed with cosign and carries an SBOM; see Verifying Releases. It holds only the tram binary on a distroless base, runs as the non-root user 65532 and starts tram server with both APIs listening on all interfaces of the container:

docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -p 50051:50051 -p 4317:4317 -p 4318:4318 ghcr.io/go-tram/tram:latest

Publish the ports the sources of your streams listen on as well, e.g. 4317 and 4318 for an OTLP source with gRPC and HTTP. Arguments replace the default command, so repeat the endpoints when adding flags, e.g. for file sync and buffers:

docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -p 4318:4318 \
  -v "$PWD/config:/config" -v tram-data:/data \
  ghcr.io/go-tram/tram:latest \
  server --http-endpoint=0.0.0.0:8080 --grpc-endpoint=0.0.0.0:50051 \
  --enable-file-sync --config-dir /config --data-dir /data

items.title: Shutdown
items.text:
On SIGTERM or SIGINT, TRAM stops taking changes to streams, waits for the changes in progress, and stops all streams in parallel. Each source stops accepting data and waits for the deliveries in progress; an OTLP source waits up to 5 seconds for its requests and then closes the connections that are left. Then the stages deliver what they still hold, e.g. a batch, and the sinks stop. TRAM waits up to 25 seconds for all of that and then exits.

Give TRAM at least that long before it is killed: Kubernetes' default terminationGracePeriodSeconds of 30 seconds is enough, and so is docker stop -t 30; Docker's default of 10 seconds is not. A delivery that is cut off is not lost for clients that retry, since they got no answer, but it may reach some sinks twice.

The directories have to be writable by the user 65532. The image has no shell; debug from another container in the same network.

items.title: Configuration Sources
items.text: Besides the API, streams can be managed from files and, on Kubernetes, from Stream resources through the operator. All of them change the same set of streams.

items.title: File Sync
items.text:
./tram server --enable-file-sync --config-dir config

Every <name>.json file in the directory describes one stream, in the same format as the API request body ({"stream": {...}}); see examples/config/ for examples. The file name, without .json, is the stream name. The sync works in both directions:

  • Adding, changing or deleting a file creates, updates or deletes the stream
  • Streams created or changed through the API or the Kubernetes operator are written to files (new files are readable only by the owner, mode 0600), and deleted streams have their file removed
  • Streams without a file are deleted when the directory is synced
  • Up to 8 streams are created, updated or deleted at once, in no particular order, so a directory with many streams loads quickly even when their sinks take long to connect
  • A stream that cannot be created or updated, e.g. because NATS is not reachable yet when TRAM starts, is tried again without its file changing: after 1 second, then with a delay that doubles up to 30 seconds, until every stream is applied. Changing a file starts over with the shortest delay. A stream that keeps failing is logged once a minute; one that is applied after failing is logged once more. A file that is invalid for good is tried again as well, so fix or remove it

items.title: Conflicts Between Configuration Sources
items.text:
TRAM holds one set of streams, and the API, the file sync and the operator all write to it. A stream of a Stream resource belongs to the resource: the operator undoes any change to it from another source right away. Any other stream belongs to no source, and whatever changed it last decides what runs, until a source writes it again. When each source writes decides how a change from another source lasts:

Source Writes a stream Removes a stream API On every request On a DELETE request File sync When a file in the directory changes, for every file that differs from its running stream; while streams fail, again after each retry delay Every running stream without a file, when the directory is synced, whichever source created it Operator When the Stream resource's spec, a secret it refers to or a config map it selects changes, when the instance starts, and when another source changed or deleted the stream of a resource When the resource is deleted

The file sync writes changes of the API and the operator back to the files, so a stream changed elsewhere keeps its file. The operator does not write back to resources. That means:

  • API change, file change, deleted file or API DELETE of a stream of a Stream resource: the operator applies the resource again right away, and with file sync, its file follows. The change has an effect only for that moment, e.g. it may restart the stream's source
  • API change to a stream with a file: written to the file, so it survives a restart. A change to the file afterwards wins over it
  • Changes of the same stream at the same moment: applied one after the other, in no defined order; the last one wins, and for a stream of a resource the operator applies the resource afterwards

A stream belongs to a resource on an instance if the instance runs the resource: its namespace is watched (--watch-namespace) and, with --engine, its spec.engineRefs name the engine. Streams under a name like <namespace>.<name> without such a resource, e.g. in a namespace the instance does not watch, are left alone.

Give every stream one source that owns it and change it only there:

  • With the operator, change streams only through Stream resources, and use the API and the files to read them
  • Use file sync together with the operator only to keep a copy of the streams on disk
  • The operator names its streams <namespace>.<name>; do not create streams with the name of a resource through the API or a file, or the operator replaces them

items.title: Kubernetes Examples
items.text:
This directory contains Kubernetes YAML configurations for deploying TRAM streams in Kubernetes environments. Each example has a corresponding JSON configuration in the ../config/ directory with the same base filename.

Every example runs on the Engine demo from examples/engine.yaml: its spec.engineRefs names it. The OTLP examples listen on ports of their own, 4318 to 4327, which the Engine declares, so all examples can run on it at once.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• Kubernetes cluster
  • NATS server or OpenTelemetry Collector deployment (depending on the example)

items.title: Install the Manager and the Engine
items.text:
From the repository root, with the Helm chart charts/tram, which installs the CRDs, the roles and the manager:

helm install tram charts/tram --namespace tram-system --create-namespace

# The Engine that runs the examples
kubectl apply -f examples/k8s/examples/engine.yaml
kubectl wait engine/demo --for=condition=Ready

Or without Helm, with the kustomization in manifests/: the CRDs in manifests/crds/, and the manager with its roles in manifests/tram-manager/, in the namespace tram-system. Apply it server-side, since the CRDs are too large for a client-side apply. From the repository it deploys the image latest; every GitHub Release has the same manifests with the release's image as tram.yaml:

kubectl apply --server-side -k manifests/
# or a release
kubectl apply --server-side -f https://github.com/go-tram/tram/releases/latest/download/tram.yaml

# The Engine that runs the examples
kubectl apply -f examples/k8s/examples/engine.yaml
kubectl wait engine/demo --for=condition=Ready

items.title: Deploy a Stream
items.text:
# Deploy a basic OTLP forwarding stream
kubectl apply -f examples/k8s/examples/otlp_basic.yaml

# Check the stream: labeled engine.tram.io/demo and mounted (column MOUNTED)
kubectl get streams --show-labels
kubectl get engines

# Or deploy every example at once, with the Engine
kubectl apply -f examples/k8s/examples/

items.title: Layout
items.text:
• examples/engine.yaml: the Engine demo, which runs every example
  • examples/: the Stream examples below

items.title: Basic OTLP Examples
items.text: These examples demonstrate using the OTLP sink in TRAM for various use cases.

items.title: otlp_basic.yaml
items.text: Purpose: Basic OTLP to OTLP forwarding - Receives OTLP data on port 4318 - Forwards to a central OTLP collector - No processing stages - JSON version: ../config/otlp_basic.json

items.title: otlp_tenant_routing.yaml
items.text: Purpose: Route the data of several tenants by a header an ingress per tenant sets - Receives OTLP on ports 4331 (HTTP) and 4332 (gRPC); the ingress of each tenant sets X-Tram-Router, which the source copies into the resource attribute tram.router.id - Rejects requests without a valid router ID before the batch, then routes each record to router.<router-id>.<signal> in NATS - Restrict the ports to the ingress controller with a NetworkPolicy, so no one sends with a header of their choice - JSON version: ../config/otlp_tenant_routing.json

items.title: otlp_grpc.yaml
items.text: Purpose: OTLP over gRPC and HTTP into one stream - Receives OTLP/gRPC on port 4317 and OTLP/HTTP on port 4329; the example Engine lists both ports, so its Service exposes them - Forwards both to a central OTLP collector - JSON version: ../config/otlp_grpc.json

items.title: otlp_debug.yaml
items.text: Purpose: OTLP into the debug sink, to see what reaches an Engine - Receives OTLP data on port 4327 - Logs every record it receives; see them with stern -l tram.io/engine=demo - No JSON version

items.title: otlp_secure.yaml
items.text: Purpose: Secure OTLP forwarding with authentication - Receives OTLP data on port 4321 - HTTPS endpoint - Bearer token authentication - Custom headers for metadata - JSON version: ../config/otlp_secure.json

items.title: otlp_insecure_dev.yaml
items.text: Purpose: Development configuration with insecure TLS - HTTPS endpoint with invalid certificate acceptance - Useful for local development and testing - Generator source for testing - JSON version: ../config/otlp_insecure_dev.json

items.title: otlp_batch.yaml

items.title: Service Discovery
items.text:
For production environments, consider using Kubernetes service discovery:

spec:
  sinks:
    - type: otlp
      name: my_sink
      from: my_source
      spec:
        url: "http://otel-collector-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local:4318"

items.title: NATS Configuration
items.text:
For NATS-based examples, configure the NATS driver of the broker source. The JetStream stream that holds the subject has to exist; TRAM creates none:

source:
  type: broker
  name: my_source
  spec:
    driver: nats
    signal: logs
    workers: 8
    nats:
      url: "nats://nats-server:4222"
      subject: "my-stream.logs"
      durable: "my-durable-consumer"

items.title: Secrets
items.text:
Keep sensitive values in a Secret in the namespace of the Stream and refer to it; the value replaces the whole field, see Secrets:

spec:
  sinks:
    - type: otlp
      name: secure_sink
      from: my_source
      spec:
        url: "https://otel-collector:443"
        headers:
          Authorization:
            valueFrom:
              secretKeyRef:
                name: otel-secrets
                key: authorization

Deploy with: 

kubectl create secret generic otel-secrets --from-literal=authorization="Bearer your-api-key-here"
kubectl apply -f your-stream.yaml

items.title: Resource Management
items.text: Streams run on the instances of an Engine, so resources and scaling are set on the Engine, for all of its Streams.

items.title: CPU/Memory Requests
items.text:
apiVersion: io.tram.core/v1alpha1
kind: Engine
metadata:
  name: high-volume
spec:
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: 500m
      memory: 512Mi
    limits:
      memory: 1Gi

items.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling
items.text:
The manager creates the HorizontalPodAutoscaler of an Engine:

apiVersion: io.tram.core/v1alpha1
kind: Engine
metadata:
  name: high-volume
spec:
  autoscaling:
    enabled: true
    minReplicas: 2
    maxReplicas: 10
    targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 70

items.title: OpenTelemetry Collector Integration
items.text:
The most common use case is forwarding to an OpenTelemetry Collector:

spec:
  sinks:
    - type: otlp
      name: otel_collector_sink
      from: source_or_stage
      spec:
        url: "http://otel-collector:4318"

items.title: NATS JetStream Integration
items.text:
For NATS-based pipelines, use the broker source and sink with the NATS driver. Set up the streams first, e.g. nats stream add input --subjects 'input.>' --defaults and nats stream add output --subjects 'output.>' --defaults:

source:
  type: broker
  name: nats_source
  spec:
    driver: nats
    signal: logs
    workers: 4
    nats:
      url: "nats://nats-server:4222"
      subject: "input.logs"
      durable: "tram-consumer"

sinks:
  - type: broker
    name: nats_sink
    from: nats_source
    spec:
      driver: nats
      nats:
        url: "nats://nats-server:4222"
      destination:
        logs: "'output.logs'"

items.title: Several Engines
items.text:
Which instances run a Stream is decided by spec.engineRefs, not by labels. To run streams in different places, e.g. per zone, node pool or team, create an Engine for each and name the Engines a Stream should run on:

apiVersion: io.tram.core/v1
kind: Stream
metadata:
  name: my-stream
spec:
  engineRefs:
    - name: zone-a
    - name: zone-b
  # ...

items.title: Canary
items.text: To try a new configuration or TRAM version on part of the traffic, run it on an Engine of its own, e.g. demo-canary with another spec.image, as a Stream with another name and engineRefs: [{name: demo-canary}]. Then send a share of the traffic to that Engine's Service, e.g. from the load balancer or the senders, and remove the Engine or the Stream when you are done.

items.title: Health Checks
items.text:
Check stream health: 

kubectl get stream my-stream -o yaml
kubectl describe stream my-stream

items.title: Logs
items.text:
View the logs of the instances of an Engine, which run its streams: 

kubectl logs -l tram.io/engine=demo --prefix

items.title: Metrics
items.text:
Every instance serves Prometheus metrics on /metrics of its HTTP API, which the Engine's Service exposes as the port http: 

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: tram-examples
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      tram.io/engine: demo
  endpoints:
    - port: http
      path: /metrics
      interval: 30s

items.title: Connection Pooling
items.text: The OTLP sink uses HTTP connection pooling by default: - Max idle connections: 100 - Idle connection timeout: 90 seconds - Max idle connections per host: 100

items.title: Batch Size Tuning
items.text:
Adjust batch sizes based on your workload:

stages:
  - type: batch
    name: batch
    from: source
    spec:
      max_records: 5000    # Increase for high throughput
      timeout: "500ms"    # Increase to allow larger batches

items.title: Timeout Configuration
items.text:
Set appropriate timeouts:

sinks:
  - type: otlp
    name: my_sink
    from: batch
    spec:
      url: "http://collector:4318"
      timeout: "60s"  # Longer timeout for large batches

items.title: Connection Issues
items.text:
Check connectivity to your endpoints. The TRAM image has no shell, so use a temporary pod in the namespace of the Engine: 

kubectl run curl --rm -it --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -v http://otel-collector:4318/v1/logs

items.title: Certificate Issues
items.text:
For HTTPS endpoints with self-signed certificates:

sinks:
  - type: otlp
    name: insecure_sink
    from: source
    spec:
      url: "https://collector:443"
      insecure: true  # Skip certificate validation

Or properly configure certificates in your cluster.

items.title: Authentication Issues
items.text:
Verify that the secrets a Stream refers to exist; a missing secret or key keeps the stream from starting and sets status.mounted to false: 

kubectl get secret otel-secrets -o jsonpath='{.data}'
kubectl get stream my-stream -o jsonpath='{.status}'

items.title: Security Best Practices
items.text:
1. Use HTTPS: Always use HTTPS in production for external endpoints
  2. TLS Certificates: Use proper TLS certificates, not insecure: true
  3. Secrets Management: Use Kubernetes Secrets for sensitive data
  4. Network Policies: Restrict access to your TRAM streams
  5. RBAC: Use appropriate RBAC roles for the TRAM operator

Example NetworkPolicy: 

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: tram-allow-endpoints
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      tram.io/engine: demo
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: otel-collector
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 4318
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: nats
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 4222

items.title: Stream Examples
items.text: This directory contains example JSON configurations for TRAM streams. The examples demonstrate various pipeline patterns including OTLP sinks, broker sources over NATS, and benchmark scenarios.

items.title: Quick Start
items.text:
All examples in this directory have corresponding Kubernetes YAML configurations in the ../k8s/ directory with the same base filename. For example:

  • config/otlp_basic.json ↔ k8s/examples/otlp_basic.yaml
  • config/benchmark_otlp_nats.json ↔ k8s/examples/benchmark_otlp_nats.yaml

items.title: Basic OTLP Examples
items.text: These examples demonstrate using the OTLP sink in TRAM for various use cases.

items.title: otlp_basic.json
items.text: Purpose: Simple OTLP to OTLP forwarding configuration. - Receives OTLP data on port 4318 - Forwards to another OTLP endpoint - No processing stages - Kubernetes version: ../k8s/examples/otlp_basic.yaml

items.title: otlp_tenant_routing.json
items.text: Purpose: Route the data of several tenants by a header an ingress per tenant sets. - Copies the header X-Tram-Router into the resource attribute tram.router.id with header_attributes, over HTTP (4331) and gRPC (4332); a value the client sent there itself is replaced - Rejects requests without a valid router ID before the batch, so one tenant's bad request does not fail a batch shared with others - Routes each record to the NATS subject router.<router-id>.<signal> - Keeps requests and batches below NATS' default max_payload of 1 MB with max_request_bytes and the batch's max_bytes, so no message is too large for the server - Kubernetes version: ../k8s/examples/otlp_tenant_routing.yaml

items.title: otlp_grpc.json
items.text: Purpose: Receive OTLP over gRPC and HTTP in one stream. - Receives OTLP/gRPC on port 4317, the default of most OpenTelemetry SDKs, and OTLP/HTTP on port 4329 - Forwards both to another OTLP endpoint - Send to it e.g. with OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4317, or from an OpenTelemetry Collector with the otlp exporter and tls.insecure: true - Kubernetes version: ../k8s/examples/otlp_grpc.yaml

items.title: otlp_secure.json
items.text: Purpose: Secure OTLP forwarding with HTTPS and authentication headers. - HTTPS endpoint - Bearer token authentication - Custom headers for metadata - Kubernetes version: ../k8s/examples/otlp_secure.yaml

items.title: otlp_insecure_dev.json
items.text: Purpose: Development configuration for HTTPS endpoints with invalid certificates. - Uses insecure: true to skip TLS certificate validation - Useful for local development and testing - Generator source for testing - Kubernetes version: ../k8s/examples/otlp_insecure_dev.yaml

items.title: otlp_batch.json
items.text: Purpose: High-throughput OTLP forwarding with batching. - Batches events for better throughput - 1000 records max per batch - 200ms timeout for batch flush - Kubernetes version: ../k8s/examples/otlp_batch.yaml

items.title: otlp_to_buffer.json and buffer_to_otlp.json
items.text: Purpose: OTLP forwarding that rides out outages of the destination, with two streams around a buffer queue. - otlp_to_buffer stores every request in the queue outbox before answering the client - buffer_to_otlp delivers the queue to the destination, retrying for up to the queue's max_age (24 hours) - Both run on the same instance, with tram server --data-dir on a persistent volume - Kubernetes version: ../k8s/examples/otlp_to_buffer.yaml and ../k8s/examples/buffer_to_otlp.yaml, on an Engine with storage

items.title: otlp_with_filters.json
items.text: Purpose: OTLP forwarding with CEL filtering. Lives in ../tests/ because it carries test cases. - Filters logs based on customer attribute - Shows how to use CEL expressions in filters - Sends filtered data to customer-specific endpoint - Kubernetes version: ../k8s/examples/otlp_with_filters.yaml

items.title: otlp_with_transform.json
items.text: Purpose: Normalize attributes with the transform stage. Lives in ../tests/ because it carries test cases. - Derives deployment.environment on the resource from the namespace, once per resource - Deletes password, renames user to user.name, truncates note and lowercases the severity into level - Its test cases show a normalized record and one the statements do not apply to, kept as it is (on_error: skip); run them with tram test ../tests/otlp_with_transform.json - Kubernetes version: ../k8s/examples/otlp_with_transform.yaml

items.title: otlp_with_validation.json
items.text: Purpose: OTLP forwarding with CEL validation. - Validates that all resources have service.name attribute - Rejects invalid data with HTTP 422 - Protects downstream systems from malformed data - Kubernetes version: ../k8s/examples/otlp_with_validation.yaml

items.title: otlp_multi_sink.json
items.text: Purpose: Multiple OTLP sinks from a single source (fan-out architecture). - Splits data into different streams using filters - Sends error/warn logs to one endpoint - Sends all data to another endpoint - Kubernetes version: ../k8s/examples/otlp_multi_sink.yaml

items.title: otlp_nats_bridge.json
items.text: Purpose: Bridges NATS JetStream to OTLP HTTP. - Consumes OTLP logs from NATS JetStream with the broker source - Uses durable consumer with multiple workers - Batches messages for efficiency - Forwards to central OTLP collector - Kubernetes version: ../k8s/examples/otlp_nats_bridge.yaml

items.title: OTLP Sink Reference
items.text:
Required Fields: - url: OTLP HTTP endpoint URL

Optional Fields: - headers: HTTP headers as key-value pairs - timeout: Request timeout as Go duration (default: 10s) - insecure: Skip TLS certificate validation (default: false)

Endpoint Paths: The OTLP sink automatically uses the correct paths: - Logs: {url}/v1/logs - Metrics: {url}/v1/metrics - Traces: {url}/v1/traces

Error Handling: - HTTP errors (non-2xx) are returned to the caller - Invalid configurations are rejected at startup - Nil events are handled gracefully - Empty events (no logs/metrics/traces) result in errors

items.title: Broker Source/Sink Reference (NATS driver)
items.text:
TRAM creates no streams: set them up before the stream starts, e.g. nats stream add input-stream --subjects 'telemetry.>' --defaults. See COMPONENTS.md for all fields.

Broker Source Fields: - driver: nats - signal: logs, metrics or traces; every message of the subject holds this signal - workers: Number of concurrent workers - nats.url, nats.subject (consumer filter), nats.stream (optional), nats.durable (optional)

Broker Sink Fields: - driver: nats - nats.url: NATS server URL - destination.logs / .metrics / .traces: CEL expressions that return the subject of each record

items.title: Kubernetes Operator
items.text: Lets TRAM run streams described by Stream custom resources (io.tram.core/v1). The operator is part of the TRAM binary and starts together with the server; it is not deployed separately.

items.title: Running
items.text:
1. Install the custom resource definition:
kubectl apply -f manifests/crds/io.tram.core_streams.yaml
  1. Start TRAM with the operator enabled:
./tram server --enable-k8s-operator

TRAM connects with the in-cluster configuration when it runs in a pod, otherwise with the KUBECONFIG environment variable or ~/.kube/config. --kubeconfig <file> selects a specific file.

  1. Create a Stream, e.g. the example in examples/k8s/:
kubectl apply -f examples/k8s/examples/otlp_basic.yaml

When TRAM runs in a cluster, its service account needs the permissions in manifests/tram-manager/rbac/engine/role.yaml (a ClusterRole named manager-role), bound with a ClusterRoleBinding. With --watch-namespace, a RoleBinding to that ClusterRole in each watched namespace is enough. The role includes reading Secret and ConfigMap resources, for references to secrets and config maps.

items.title: Selecting Streams
items.text:
By default every TRAM instance with the operator enabled runs every Stream resource in the cluster. Two flags limit an instance to some of them; when both are set, a resource has to match both:

Flag Description --watch-namespace Comma-separated namespaces whose Stream resources the instance runs, e.g. tram-validation,tram-bridge --engine Engine whose Stream resources the instance runs: those whose spec.engineRefs name it. tram manager sets it on the instances of each Engine
  • A resource that no instance selects runs nowhere, and its status.mounted is not set
  • With --engine, the instance watches only the resources labeled engine.tram.io/<engine>, which tram manager derives from spec.engineRefs, and runs only those whose spec.engineRefs still name the engine. Removing the reference stops the stream on the engine's instances; adding it starts the stream
  • --engine only assigns streams to instances, it is no access control. Anyone who can create a Stream in a watched namespace can name any engine. Use --watch-namespace and RBAC to restrict who can run streams on an instance

items.title: Development
items.text:
Path Content api/v1/stream_types.go The Stream type and its kubebuilder markers api/v1/zz_generated.deepcopy.go Generated api/v1/engine_labels.go The engine labels derived from spec.engineRefs internal/controller/stream_controller.go Reconciliation and the RBAC markers api/v1alpha1/engine_types.go The Engine type and its kubebuilder markers internal/engines/ The controllers of tram manager: engine_controller.go runs Engines, resources.go builds their resources, stream_controller.go derives engine labels and status.engines; with their RBAC markers operator.go Starts the controller manager inside TRAM manager.go Starts the controller manager of tram manager, with leader election; caches only the resources it generates

After changing types or markers, regenerate the deepcopy code and the manifests with controller-gen v0.22.0. They write the CRDs to manifests/crds/ and the roles to manifests/tram-manager/rbac/ at the repository root, and the same files to the Helm chart charts/tram, the CRDs to its crds/ directory and the roles to templates/tram-manager/rbac/:

go generate ./internal/adapters/k8scrd/...

items.title: Engines
items.text:
An Engine (io.tram.core/v1alpha1) is a group of TRAM instances that tram manager runs as a Deployment, or as a StatefulSet if it has storage for buffers. A Stream names the engines that run it in spec.engineRefs, and every instance of each of them runs it:

apiVersion: io.tram.core/v1alpha1
kind: Engine
metadata:
  name: telemetry-hub-mapper
  namespace: tram-nats-13
spec:
  replicas: 3                       # used while autoscaling is disabled
  image: registry.example.com/tram:1.14.0   # optional, defaults to the manager's --engine-image
  imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
  resources:
    requests: { cpu: "4", memory: 8Gi }
    limits: { memory: 12Gi }
  autoscaling:                      # optional
    enabled: true                   # default false
    minReplicas: 3                  # required while enabled
    maxReplicas: 24                 # required while enabled, >= minReplicas
    targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 70   # default 80
  disruptionBudget:                 # optional, one of minAvailable and maxUnavailable
    maxUnavailable: 1
  ports:                            # ports the HTTP sources of its Streams may listen on
    - name: otlp-http
      port: 4318
  service:
    type: ClusterIP                 # default
  runtime:                          # maps to flags of tram server
    logLevel: info                  # --log-level, default info
    api:
      httpPort: 8080                # --http-endpoint, also serves /metrics; default 8080
      grpcPort: 50051               # --grpc-endpoint; default 50051
    pprof:                          # optional, --pprof-endpoint on the pod's localhost
      port: 6060
  podTemplate:                      # pod-level settings only
    metadata:
      labels: { team: telemetry }
      annotations: { prometheus.io/scrape: "true", prometheus.io/port: "8080" }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 # TRAM needs up to 25s to stop its streams; see Shutdown
      priorityClassName: telemetry-high
      nodeSelector: { node-pool: telemetry }
      tolerations: [...]
      affinity: {...}
      topologySpreadConstraints: [...]
      securityContext: {...}
      imagePullSecrets: [...]
  storage:                          # optional, see Storage for buffers
    size: 20Gi                      # cannot be changed
    storageClassName: fast-ssd      # optional, cannot be changed
    mountPath: /var/lib/tram        # default
    drainResources:                 # default: requests 50m CPU, 128Mi; the instances' limits
      requests: { cpu: 50m, memory: 128Mi }

apiVersion: io.tram.core/v1
kind: Stream
metadata:
  name: resource-to-router-audit
  namespace: tram-nats-13
spec:
  engineRefs:
    - name: telemetry-hub-mapper
  source: ...

The tram container of the instances, and of the drain Jobs, runs as non-root with a read-only root file system, without privilege escalation or capabilities, and with the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile; these settings cannot be changed. Temporary files, e.g. those of SQLite, go to an empty directory mounted at /tmp. podTemplate.spec.securityContext sets the pod-level context, e.g. another fsGroup.

The Helm chart charts/tram or the kustomization in manifests/ deploys the manager with the CRDs and roles, and examples/k8s/examples/ holds an Engine and Streams that run on it.

What the manager creates for an Engine, and how its instances find their Streams:

flowchart LR
    manager["tram manager"]
    subgraph ns["Engine's namespace"]
        engine[/"Engine blue-line"/]
        stream[/"Stream<br/>spec.engineRefs: blue-line"/]
        refs[/"Secrets and ConfigMaps<br/>the Stream refers to"/]
        workload["Deployment,<br/>or StatefulSet with storage"]
        others["Service, ServiceAccount, RoleBinding,<br/>PodDisruptionBudget, HorizontalPodAutoscaler"]
        instances["TRAM instances<br/>tram server<br/>--engine blue-line"]
    end
    manager -- watches --> engine
    manager -- creates --> workload
    manager -- creates --> others
    manager -- "labels engine.tram.io/blue-line" --> stream
    workload -- runs --> instances
    instances -- "watch Streams labeled for blue-line, run them" --> stream
    instances -. read .-> refs

items.title: The Manager
items.text:
tram manager runs no streams. It runs one Deployment or StatefulSet per Engine, and it labels every Stream engine.tram.io/<name> (with an empty value) for each engine its spec.engineRefs name; the instances of an engine select the key, e.g. kubectl get streams -l engine.tram.io/engine-1. Run it once per cluster, or as several replicas, of which one at a time works:

./tram manager --engine-image registry.example.com/tram:1.14.0

items.title: RBAC
items.text:
Role File Bound to tram-manager manifests/tram-manager/rbac/manager/role.yaml The manager's service account, with a ClusterRoleBinding (a RoleBinding per namespace with --watch-namespace). Engines, Streams, the generated resources including StatefulSets, drain Jobs and volume claims, reading pods, leader election, and bind on manager-role manager-role manifests/tram-manager/rbac/engine/role.yaml Each Engine's service account, by the manager, in the Engine's namespace

Both ClusterRoles have to exist. With another --engine-cluster-role, grant the manager bind on that role instead.

items.title: Helm Chart
items.text: Deploys tram manager, which runs every Engine resource as a Deployment (or StatefulSet) of TRAM instances in the Engine's namespace, and the Engine and Stream CRDs. Engines and Streams are resources you create, not part of the chart; see Engines and the examples in examples/k8s/examples/.

items.title: Install
items.text:
Every release publishes the chart to oci://ghcr.io/go-tram/charts/tram, with the release's version as both the chart version and the app version:

helm install tram oci://ghcr.io/go-tram/charts/tram --namespace tram-system --create-namespace

Without --version, Helm installs the latest release; add e.g. --version 0.0.19 to pin one.

The chart is attached to the GitHub Release as tram-<version>.tgz as well. From the repository, the chart has the version 0.0.0 and deploys the image latest, which is the latest release:

helm install tram charts/tram --namespace tram-system --create-namespace

Then create an Engine and a Stream that runs on it:

kubectl apply -f examples/k8s/examples/engine.yaml
kubectl wait engine/demo --for=condition=Ready
kubectl apply -f examples/k8s/examples/otlp_debug.yaml
kubectl get engines,streams

The chart deploys ghcr.io/go-tram/tram in the chart's appVersion, the release's version, by default. If the package is private, pass a pull secret with imagePullSecrets; for an image of your own, set image.repository and image.tag. The manager runs the Engines' instances, and their drain Jobs, with the same image, unless manager.engineImage names another; an Engine's own image overrides both.

items.title: What It Creates
items.text:
Resource Name Purpose Deployment <fullname> tram manager, two replicas with leader election by default; the lease is in the release's namespace ServiceAccount <fullname> The manager's identity ClusterRole tram-manager What the manager may do: run Engines (Deployments, StatefulSets, Services, ServiceAccounts, …) and label Streams ClusterRoleBinding <fullname> Binds tram-manager to the manager's service account. With manager.watchNamespaces, a RoleBinding of the same name in each of these namespaces and in the release's namespace instead, so the manager has no rights elsewhere PodDisruptionBudget <fullname> Keeps one replica of the manager running while nodes are drained; only with more than one replica PodMonitor <fullname>-engines Optional: lets the Prometheus operator scrape /metrics of every Engine's instances ClusterRole manager-role What the Engines' instances may do: read their Streams, Secrets and ConfigMaps. The manager binds it to the service account of every Engine, in the Engine's namespace, and may bind no other role CustomResourceDefinitions engines.io.tram.core, streams.io.tram.core The Engine and Stream resources; kept on uninstall

<fullname> is the release name, with -tram appended unless the release name contains tram; fullnameOverride replaces it. The ClusterRoles and CRDs are cluster-wide and have fixed names, so install the chart once per cluster.

items.title: Generated Templates
items.text: The CRDs in crds/ and the ClusterRoles in templates/tram-manager/rbac/ are generated by controller-gen from the //go:generate directives in internal/adapters/k8scrd/operator.go, which write the same files to manifests/. Do not edit them by hand; run task generate. The other templates are written by hand.

items.title: CRDs
items.text:
The CRDs are in Helm's crds/ directory, so Helm handles them apart from the templates: helm install creates them if they do not exist yet, while helm upgrade neither creates nor updates them and helm uninstall leaves them. helm template leaves them out unless you pass --include-crds.

If you manage the CRDs yourself, e.g. from manifests/crds/, install the chart without them with --skip-crds, or skipCrds: true in the Helm source of an Argo CD Application.

Since helm upgrade does not touch the CRDs, apply the ones of the new version before upgrading the chart, server-side, as they are too large for a client-side apply:

helm show crds oci://ghcr.io/go-tram/charts/tram --version <version> | kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts -f -
helm upgrade tram oci://ghcr.io/go-tram/charts/tram --version <version> --namespace tram-system

items.title: Uninstall
items.text:
helm uninstall tram --namespace tram-system

This removes the manager and its RBAC but keeps the CRDs, and with them every Engine and Stream of the cluster and the Engines' Deployments and StatefulSets, which run on without a manager until you install it again. To remove everything, delete the Engines first, so the manager drains their buffers and cleans up, then the CRDs:

kubectl delete engines --all -A
kubectl delete crd engines.io.tram.core streams.io.tram.core

items.title: Values
items.text: Key Default Description replicaCount 2 Replicas of the manager; with leader election, one works at a time image.repository ghcr.io/go-tram/tram Image of the manager image.tag "" Tag of the image; defaults to the chart's appVersion image.pullPolicy IfNotPresent Pull policy of the image imagePullSecrets [] Secrets to pull the manager's image, e.g. [{name: ghcr}] nameOverride "" Replaces the chart name in the resource names fullnameOverride "" Replaces the full name of the resources manager.watchNamespaces [] Namespaces whose Engines and Streams the manager handles; empty for all. Set, the manager gets RoleBindings in these namespaces only manager.engineImage "" Image of the Engines' instances and drain Jobs; defaults to the manager's image manager.leaderElect true Let only one replica work at a time; leave it on with more than one replica manager.logLevel info Log level: debug, info, warn or error manager.extraArgs [] More arguments for tram manager manager.extraEnv [] Environment variables of the manager's container serviceAccount.create true Create the manager's service account serviceAccount.name "" Name of the service account; defaults to the full name serviceAccount.annotations {} Annotations of the service account podAnnotations {} Annotations of the manager's pods podLabels {} Labels of the manager's pods, besides the chart's podSecurityContext non-root as 65532, RuntimeDefault seccomp Security context of the pods; the image's user nonroot is 65532, which runAsNonRoot needs as a number securityContext no privilege escalation, read-only root file system, no capabilities Security context of the container resources requests 100m CPU and 128Mi, limit 256Mi Resources of the container priorityClassName "" Priority class of the pods nodeSelector, tolerations, affinity, topologySpreadConstraints empty Scheduling of the pods podDisruptionBudget.enabled true Create a PodDisruptionBudget for the manager when replicaCount is above 1 podDisruptionBudget.maxUnavailable 1 Replicas of the manager a disruption may take down engineMetrics.podMonitor.enabled false Create a PodMonitor for the Engines' instances; needs the Prometheus operator's CRDs engineMetrics.podMonitor.interval 30s Scrape interval engineMetrics.podMonitor.labels {} Labels of the PodMonitor, e.g. what your Prometheus selects on

items.title: Storage for Buffers
items.text:
The buffer sink and source keep their queues on the instance's disk. With spec.storage, the manager runs the Engine as a StatefulSet in which every instance has a volume of its own (ReadWriteOnce, claim data-tram-engine-<engine>-<ordinal>) mounted as its data directory. Without it, the Engine runs as a Deployment, and Streams with a buffer sink or source do not run on it. Every such Stream reports per Engine in status.engines[].conditions whether it can: StorageAvailable is True, or False with reason EngineHasNoStorage, or StorageMigrating while the instances move to a StatefulSet.

Rule: buffered events are never discarded before their max_age because of a change in Kubernetes. The manager keeps every volume either with a running instance or with a drain Job, and deletes a volume only when its drain Job finished, or once everything on it has expired.

The life of a volume:

stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    state "Used by its instance" as used
    state "Drained by a Job" as draining
    state "Kept, drain failed" as failed
    [*] --> used: instance starts
    used --> draining: instance goes, by scale-down, removed storage or a deleted Engine
    draining --> used: scale-up stops the Job
    draining --> failed: Job fails after its retries
    failed --> draining: Job deleted by hand
    draining --> [*]: queues empty or expired, VolumeDrained
    draining --> [*]: Job older than largest max_age plus 1h, VolumeExpired
    used --> [*]: instance goes while the Engine has the discard annotation, VolumeDiscarded
    draining --> [*]: discard annotation set, VolumeDiscarded
What happens What the manager does storage is added Starts a StatefulSet with as many instances as the Deployment, next to it; both serve meanwhile. Once the StatefulSet is ready, the Service selects only its instances (label tram.io/storage: "true"), then the Deployment is deleted, so no request reaches an instance without storage. Migrating is True meanwhile storage is removed Waits while Streams still write to buffers on the Engine, i.e. have a buffer sink and are not suspended: Reconciled is False with reason StorageInUse, naming them. Once none writes any more, starts a Deployment, and when it is ready, deletes the StatefulSet; its volumes stay and are drained through the reading Streams, see Removing storage Scaling down, also by the autoscaler The volume of an instance that goes stays and is drained Scaling up while a volume is drained Stops the drain Job; the instance continues with its volume The Engine is deleted Keeps it (finalizer tram.io/drain-buffers) until all its volumes are drained, after stopping its instances

A drain Job (tram-drain-<random>, labels tram.io/drain=<engine> and tram.io/ordinal=<n>) runs tram drain with the volume mounted: it loads the Engine's Streams and runs only those that read from a buffer, also suspended ones, and treats all others as suspended, so nothing writes to the volume any more. It ends once every queue is empty or holds only expired events, also queues no Stream reads any more, so it takes at most about the largest max_age after the instance stopped. Its pod is not selected by the Engine's Service or disruption budget and uses storage.drainResources. When it is done, the volume is deleted, and the Job stays for an hour, so its logs show what it delivered (kubectl logs -l tram.io/drain=<engine>). Its finished pod still uses the volume, so the claim stays Terminating until the Job goes; if an instance needs a volume of the same name before, because storage was added back or the Engine scaled up, the manager deletes the Job, and with it its logs, right away. If a drain Job fails after its retries, the volume is kept and the Engine's Draining condition says so; delete the Job to try again. If a drain Job never finishes, e.g. because its volume cannot be attached, the volume is deleted once the Job is older than the largest max_age of the Engine's buffer sinks (at least 24 hours) plus one hour, since everything on it has expired by then.

Deleting or suspending a Stream discards nothing: what its buffer sink wrote waits in the queue until a reading Stream delivers it or it expires, like messages of a broker without a consumer.

items.title: Removing storage
items.text:
Removing storage ends the buffers on the Engine, so the manager asks the Streams' authors to stop writing first, and delivers what the volumes still hold through the reading Streams:

  1. Suspend the Streams that write to buffers (spec.suspended: true), or remove their buffer sinks. Their sources stop, so their clients can no longer send to them. Keep the Streams that read from the buffers
  2. Remove spec.storage from the Engine. The manager starts a Deployment; once it is ready, it deletes the StatefulSet
  3. A drain Job per volume runs the reading Streams against it and delivers through their sinks. A volume is deleted once its queues are empty, or their events expired because the destination stayed down
  4. Delete the reading Streams, or keep them for when the Engine gets storage again

On instances without storage, Streams with a buffer sink or source do not run: they are not mounted (status.mounted is false), and report StorageAvailable=False per Engine.

The manager records events on the Engine (kubectl describe engine <name>): VolumeDraining when a drain Job starts, VolumeDrained when it is done, VolumeExpired when a volume was deleted after the drain deadline, and VolumeDiscarded when the discard annotation deleted it, and VolumeReleased when it deleted a kept drain Job early so an instance gets its volume.

The Engine's status shows the workload (status.workload), the number of volumes (status.volumes) and of volumes being drained (status.drainingVolumes), and the conditions Migrating and Draining.

To give up buffered events on purpose, annotate the Engine with tram.io/discard-buffers: "true" before or while deleting it; its volumes are deleted at once.

Limits:

  • Deleting a namespace discards buffered events. Kubernetes deletes everything in it, and nothing can be created in it any more, so no drain Job can run. Delete the Streams and Engines first and wait until they are gone
  • size and storageClassName cannot be changed; resize the volumes by hand if the storage class allows it
  • When a node fails, the StatefulSet does not start its instance elsewhere until the pod is gone; the volume is delivered once the instance runs again
  • PVCs need Kubernetes 1.32 or later for persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy; older clusters ignore it, and the manager's drains still delete volumes only when they are done

items.title: Stream Resources
items.text:
apiVersion: io.tram.core/v1
kind: Stream
metadata:
  name: test-stream
  namespace: default
spec:
  source:
    name: generator
    type: generator
    spec:
      interval: 2s
  stages:
    - name: delay
      type: delay
      from: generator
      spec:
        delay: 1s
  sinks:
    - name: debug
      type: debug
      from: delay

spec has the same structure as the stream object of the HTTP API, without name. Each component's spec is passed to the component as it is, so numbers, booleans and nested objects keep their types; see COMPONENTS.md for the options of each component.

items.title: Secrets
items.text:
Any value in a component's spec can come from a Secret in the namespace of the Stream, like environment variables of a pod:

  sinks:
    - name: otlp
      type: otlp
      from: in
      spec:
        url: https://collector.example.com:4318
        headers:
          Authorization:
            valueFrom:
              secretKeyRef:
                name: otlp-auth   # Secret in the namespace of the Stream
                key: token        # e.g. "Bearer ..."
  • The value replaces the whole object as a string, so a header needs its complete value in the secret, e.g. Bearer ...
  • The stream runs with the values, but TRAM shows only the references: the API and the files of the file sync never contain a secret's value. A component may still name a value in an error it logs, e.g. an invalid URL, so keep secrets out of values that components check, like URLs
  • Changing a secret restarts the streams that refer to it with the new value. TRAM watches only the metadata of secrets and reads a value when it applies a stream, so values are not kept in its cache
  • A missing secret or key keeps the stream from starting and sets status.mounted to false; the stream starts once the secret is there. A malformed reference, e.g. without key, fails for good until the resource is fixed
  • References work only in Stream resources. Streams from the API or the file sync are passed on unchanged, so they cannot read secrets or config maps

items.title: Config Maps
items.text:
A value in a component's spec can also be the merged data of all ConfigMap resources in the namespace of the Stream that a label selector matches. This keeps large tables, e.g. the table of a value_map stage, out of the Stream resource and lets them grow beyond the size limit of a single Kubernetes object:

  stages:
    - name: router
      type: value_map
      from: in
      spec:
        source_attr: tenant.id
        target_attr: router.id
        default: unassigned
        table:
          valueFrom:
            configMapSelector:        # like the selector of a Deployment
              matchLabels:
                tram.io/table: tenant-routing
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: tenant-routing-router-1
  labels:
    tram.io/table: tenant-routing
data:
  tenant-a: router-1
  tenant-b: router-1
  • The selector takes matchLabels and matchExpressions, at least one of them. The value is an object with the keys and values of data of every matching config map; binaryData is ignored
  • Split a table over as many config maps as needed, e.g. one per router. A key may be in several of them only with the same value. Different values are a conflict: the error names the key and both config maps
  • Creating, changing or deleting a matching config map, or changing labels so that it starts or stops matching, applies the new table. Like with a changed spec, only stages and sinks are replaced; the source keeps running. As with secrets, TRAM watches only the metadata of config maps and reads their data when it applies a stream
  • No matching config map, or a conflict, keeps the stream from starting and sets status.mounted to false. A stream that already runs keeps running with its last table until the config maps are fixed. A malformed selector, e.g. an empty one, which would match every config map of the namespace, fails for good until the resource is fixed
  • The merged table exists only in TRAM's memory: it is never written to a Kubernetes object, so only each config map on its own is bound by the size limit. The API and the file sync show the selector, not the table
  • Every TRAM instance that runs the stream holds the whole table, and every reconcile reads all matching config maps. Keep tables of hundreds of thousands of entries in mind when sizing memory

items.title: Behavior
items.text:
• Names: a resource runs as the TRAM stream <namespace>.<name>, e.g. default.test-stream, so resources with the same name in different namespaces do not collide. The stream can be read through the API under that name
  • Changes: the stream is created or updated when the resource's spec, a secret it refers to, or a config map it selects changes. Status updates and periodic resyncs do not restart it. An instance builds up to 8 Streams at once, in no particular order, e.g. when it starts, so a new replica runs all its Streams sooner; one Stream is never reconciled twice at the same time
  • Status: status.mounted is true once an instance loaded the stream, also while it is suspended (spec.suspended, which defaults to false), and false if building it failed, e.g. because of an invalid component spec, or if the instance cannot run it, e.g. a stream with a buffer on an Engine without storage. Failed builds are retried with increasing delays. If the stream's source stops later, TRAM restarts the stream on its own; status.mounted stays true meanwhile. kubectl get streams shows both as the columns Mounted and Suspended. Until version 0.0.19 the field was called status.active
  • Deletion: deleting the resource deletes the stream
  • Ownership: the operator reads Stream resources; it does not write streams back as resources. A resource owns its stream: a change or deletion of the stream through the API or the file sync is undone right away, so with the operator, manage streams through Stream resources and use the API to read them. File sync, in contrast, works in both directions
  • Scope: the operator watches Stream resources in all namespaces, or in the namespaces from --watch-namespace, and with --engine only those whose spec.engineRefs name the engine; see Selecting Streams. There is no leader election, so every TRAM instance with the operator enabled runs every Stream resource it selects
  • Access: creating a Stream lets its author open ports on the TRAM pod and send data anywhere TRAM can reach, from any namespace. Its author can also have TRAM read any secret or config map in the Stream's namespace and send the value along, e.g. as a header to their own URL. Grant create on streams.io.tram.core only to users you would also trust with the TRAM deployment and with the secrets and config maps of that namespace; see Security
  • File sync: with --enable-file-sync, streams created by the operator are also written to the configuration directory. Editing or deleting such a file is undone right away, like a change through the API; see Conflicts Between Configuration Sources

items.title: Contributing
items.text: Thank you for your interest in contributing to TRAM! This document provides guidelines for contributing to the project.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• Go 1.26+
  • Task, recommended, to run the common commands (see Tasks)
  • Docker or Podman, optional, for the container image, a local NATS server and the tests and benchmarks that use Testcontainers

Only needed to regenerate code (task generate), installed with task tools:

  • buf and the protoc plugins used in buf.gen.yaml
  • controller-gen for the Kubernetes CRD and deepcopy code

Only needed to check the Helm chart (task chart:lint): Helm, and kubeconform, installed with task tools.

items.title: Install Dependencies
items.text:
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/go-tram/tram.git tram
cd tram

# Install Go dependencies
go mod download

# Code generators, golangci-lint and benchstat, in the versions the
# generated code was made with (see the versions in Taskfile.yml)
task tools

# Optional: NATS with JetStream for the broker source and sink
task nats:up

items.title: Tasks
items.text:
Taskfile.yml holds the common commands. task lists them, task --summary <name> explains one, and arguments after -- are passed on, e.g. task test:unit -- -run TestBatch -v.

Task What it does task build / task run Build the binary, or run the server (task run -- --enable-file-sync) task check Lint, unit and end-to-end tests: what a change should pass task ci / task ci:lint / task ci:test / task ci:containers / task ci:envtest What the CI workflows run: the pinned golangci-lint and govulncheck (ci:lint), unit and end-to-end tests without the broker packages (ci:test), the broker tests against containers (ci:containers), and the operator tests against a real API server (ci:envtest) task vuln Checks the code and its dependencies for known vulnerabilities with govulncheck; fails only on vulnerable code that TRAM calls task test:all task check plus the container and operator (envtest) tests; fails instead of skipping if Podman/Docker or setup-envtest is missing task test All tests; tests that need containers are skipped without Docker or Podman task test:unit / task test:e2e Unit tests only, or the end-to-end tests that need no containers task test:containers End-to-end tests against NATS, Kafka and Artemis (AMQP) in containers; fails if no container runtime runs task test:envtest Kubernetes operator tests against a real API server and etcd; downloads them on first use task test:upgrade Upgrades from the latest release to this repository in a kind cluster and checks that buffered events survive; needs kind, helm and kubectl task test:cover All tests with coverage, written to coverage.out task lint / task fmt golangci-lint (including go vet), or format with its configured formatters task generate Regenerate protobuf, gateway and swagger code and the Kubernetes CRD task bench Benchmarks, e.g. task bench BENCH=Batch PKG=./internal/adapters/stage/batch/ task bench:compare Compare two benchmark outputs with benchstat task bench:report Run all benchmarks and regenerate BENCHMARK.md task image:build / task image:run Build the container image tram:dev, or run it with the APIs on localhost task nats:up / task nats:down Start or stop a local NATS server with JetStream task k8s:crd Install the Stream CRD into the current Kubernetes context task tools Install the code generators, golangci-lint, benchstat and setup-envtest task release:next / release:patch / release:minor / release:major Tag the next version on main and push it, which publishes the image (see Releases)

Container tasks use Podman if it is installed and Docker otherwise; set CONTAINER_TOOL=docker to choose. With Podman, the test and benchmark tasks also set up Testcontainers for the Podman machine (see Benchmarks).

The sections below show the underlying commands.

items.title: Build the Project
items.text:
# Build the main application
go build -o tram ./cmd/tram

# Build all packages
go build ./...

items.title: Run the Service
items.text:
# Start the service
./tram server

# Or with file-based config sync
./tram server --enable-file-sync -c config

items.title: Generate Code
items.text:
# Generate all code: protobuf and swagger (buf), Kubernetes CRD and deepcopy (controller-gen)
go generate ./...

items.title: Update API Definitions
items.text:
When updating the API:

  1. Modify the .proto files in api/proto/stream/v1/
  2. Regenerate code: 
    go generate ./...
  3. The swagger file in api/swagger/ is updated automatically

items.title: Project Structure
items.text:
tram/
├── api/
│   ├── proto/stream/v1/stream.proto  # API definition

items.title: Adding New Components
items.text: TRAM is designed to be easily extensible. Each component is a package in internal/adapters/{source|stage|sink}/<name>/ that embeds the matching base type and is registered in the factory next to it.

items.title: Common Patterns
items.text:
1. Define a Spec type for the configuration. base.New decodes the stream's spec into it and checks its validate tags (go-playground/validator); there is no Validate() method
  2. Implement the component by embedding base.Source[Spec], base.Stage[Spec] or base.Sink[Spec]. Checks the tags cannot express, like parsing durations, belong into New, so an invalid spec fails when the stream is created
  3. Register it in the switch of factory.go in a new branch
  4. Document it in COMPONENTS.md

Rules all components follow:

  • Events are read-only. One event is passed to all branches concurrently. To change data, build a new event, e.g. with domain.FilterLogs, FilterMetrics and FilterSpans, which share unchanged records instead of copying them
  • Notify returns the delivery result. Return an error wrapping domain.ErrEventRejected when retrying the same data cannot succeed; sources then reject it (OTLP: HTTP 422, broker: reject the message). Any other error is treated as temporary (OTLP: HTTP 503, broker: redelivery)
  • Notify may block while it delivers the event downstream, or when waiting is its documented purpose (batch, delay). It has to return when ctx is done
  • Lifecycle: New may acquire resources such as connections. Stop is called exactly once and must release them; it may be called without Run, e.g. when building the stream failed. The core stops the source first, waits for its Run to return, and then stops stages and sinks from the root down
  • Updates: when an update changes only stages or sinks, the source keeps running. The core builds the new stages and sinks, switches the source over with SetSubscribers, which waits until no event is delivered to the old ones anymore, and then stops the old stages and sinks. Stages and sinks therefore have to be independent of a particular source instance

items.title: Adding a New Source
items.text: Sources have no Notify; they implement Run and Stop. The base type provides Name, Spec, Subscribe, SetSubscribers and NotifySubscribers.

items.title: 1. Create the Spec
items.text:
// internal/adapters/source/heartbeat/spec.go
package heartbeat

type Spec struct {
    Interval string `json:"interval" validate:"required"`
    Message  string `json:"message" validate:"required"`
}

items.title: 2. Implement the Source
items.text:
// internal/adapters/source/heartbeat/heartbeat.go
package heartbeat

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log/slog"
    "sync"
    "time"

    "github.com/go-tram/tram/internal/adapters/source/base"
    "github.com/go-tram/tram/internal/core/domain"
    "github.com/go-playground/validator/v10"
    commonpb "go.opentelemetry.io/proto/otlp/common/v1"
    logspb "go.opentelemetry.io/proto/otlp/logs/v1"
)

const Type = "heartbeat"

type Heartbeat struct {
    *base.Source[Spec]
    logger   *slog.Logger
    interval time.Duration
    shutdown chan struct{}
    stopOnce sync.Once
}

// New takes a logger because Run logs; components that do not log leave it out.
func New(source domain.SourceSpec, validator *validator.Validate, logger *slog.Logger) (*Heartbeat, error) {
    // Decodes the spec and checks its validate tags.
    base, err := base.New[Spec](source.Name, source.Spec, validator)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    // Checks the tags cannot express belong here too, so an invalid spec
    // fails when the stream is created.
    interval, err := time.ParseDuration(base.Spec().Interval)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid interval: %w", err)
    }

    return &Heartbeat{
        Source:   base,
        logger:   logger,
        interval: interval,
        shutdown: make(chan struct{}),
    }, nil
}

// Run produces events until Stop is called or ctx is cancelled.
func (h *Heartbeat) Run(ctx context.Context) error {
    ticker := time.NewTicker(h.interval)
    defer ticker.Stop()

    for {
        select {
        case <-h.shutdown:
            return nil
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-ticker.C:
            event := &domain.Event{Logs: &logspb.LogsData{ResourceLogs: []*logspb.ResourceLogs{{
                ScopeLogs: []*logspb.ScopeLogs{{LogRecords: []*logspb.LogRecord{{
                    TimeUnixNano: uint64(time.Now().UnixNano()),
                    Body:         &commonpb.AnyValue{Value: &commonpb.AnyValue_StringValue{StringValue: h.Spec().Message}},
                }}}},
            }}}}

            // Returns once all children have processed the event.
            if err := h.NotifySubscribers(ctx, event); err != nil {
                h.logger.ErrorContext(ctx, "Could not deliver event",
                    slog.String("source", h.Name()), slog.Any("error", err))
            }
        }
    }
}

// Stop makes Run return. It may be called without Run, e.g. when building
// the stream failed, and must release everything New acquired.
func (h *Heartbeat) Stop() error {
    h.stopOnce.Do(func() { close(h.shutdown) })
    return nil
}

var _ domain.Source = (*Heartbeat)(nil)

items.text: Stages implement Notify and pass events on with NotifySubscribers. The base type provides Name, From, Spec, Subscribe and a Stop that does nothing.
