items.title: 2. Implement the Stage
items.text:
// internal/adapters/stage/severity/severity.go
package severity

import (
    "context"

    "github.com/go-tram/tram/internal/adapters/stage/base"
    "github.com/go-tram/tram/internal/core/domain"
    "github.com/go-playground/validator/v10"
    commonpb "go.opentelemetry.io/proto/otlp/common/v1"
    logspb "go.opentelemetry.io/proto/otlp/logs/v1"
    resourcepb "go.opentelemetry.io/proto/otlp/resource/v1"
)

const Type = "severity"

type Severity struct {
    *base.Stage[Spec]
}

func New(stage domain.StageSpec, validator *validator.Validate) (*Severity, error) {
    base, err := base.New[Spec](stage.Name, stage.From, stage.Spec, validator)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return &Severity{Stage: base}, nil
}

// Notify keeps the log records with at least the configured severity. The
// event is shared with sibling branches, so it is never modified; FilterLogs
// builds a new payload and shares the kept records.
func (s *Severity) Notify(ctx context.Context, event *domain.Event) error {
    logs, err := domain.FilterLogs(event.Logs, func(_ *resourcepb.Resource, _ *commonpb.InstrumentationScope, record *logspb.LogRecord) (bool, error) {
        return int(record.SeverityNumber) >= s.Spec().Min, nil
    })
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    filtered := *event
    filtered.Logs = logs
    if filtered.RecordCount() == 0 {
        return nil
    }
    return s.NotifySubscribers(ctx, &filtered)
}

var _ domain.Stage = (*Severity)(nil)

items.title: Adding a New Sink
items.text: Sinks implement Notify. The base type provides Name, From, Spec and a Stop that does nothing.

items.title: 1. Create the Spec
items.text:
// internal/adapters/sink/webhook/spec.go
package webhook

type Spec struct {
    URL string `json:"url" validate:"required,url"`
}

items.title: 2. Implement the Sink
items.text:
// internal/adapters/sink/webhook/webhook.go
package webhook

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "time"

    "github.com/go-tram/tram/internal/adapters/sink/base"
    "github.com/go-tram/tram/internal/core/domain"
    "github.com/go-playground/validator/v10"
    "google.golang.org/protobuf/proto"
)

const Type = "webhook"

type Webhook struct {
    *base.Sink[Spec]
    client *http.Client
}

func New(sink domain.SinkSpec, validator *validator.Validate) (*Webhook, error) {
    base, err := base.New[Spec](sink.Name, sink.From, sink.Spec, validator)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return &Webhook{
        Sink:   base,
        client: &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second},
    }, nil
}

// Notify posts the logs of an event as OTLP/HTTP protobuf. The returned
// error tells the source whether retrying can help.
func (w *Webhook) Notify(ctx context.Context, event *domain.Event) error {
    if event.Logs == nil {
        return nil
    }
    body, err := proto.Marshal(event.Logs)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("marshal logs: %w", err)
    }

    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, w.Spec().URL, bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("create request: %w", err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/x-protobuf")

    resp, err := w.client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("send logs: %w", err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    switch {
    case resp.StatusCode >= 500:
        // Temporary: the source may retry, e.g. the broker source has the message redelivered.
        return fmt.Errorf("send logs: %s", resp.Status)
    case resp.StatusCode >= 400:
        // Permanent: retrying the same data cannot succeed.
        return fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", domain.ErrEventRejected, resp.Status)
    }
    return nil
}

func (w *Webhook) Stop() error {
    w.client.CloseIdleConnections()
    return nil
}

var _ domain.Sink = (*Webhook)(nil)

items.title: Before Submitting
items.text:
1. Generate code: Make sure all code is generated 

    task generate

  2. Format code: Use the formatters configured for golangci-lint 

    task fmt

  3. Lint and test: Ensure linting and all tests pass 

    task check

  4. Test against NATS: If you changed the broker source or sink or a driver, also run the container tests 

    task test:containers

  5. Test the operator: If you changed the Kubernetes operator, also run the envtest tests 

    task test:envtest

task test:all runs steps 3 to 5 in one go.

items.title: Pull Request Requirements
items.text:
1. Conventional title: The title follows Conventional Commits, e.g. feat(k8s): drain buffers on scale-down, with one of the types feat, fix, perf, refactor, docs, test, build, ci, chore or revert. Pull requests are squash-merged with their title as the commit message, so a check blocks the merge until the title conforms
  2. Detailed description: Explain the changes and why they're needed
  3. Small, focused changes: One logical change per PR
  4. Proper commit messages: Follow Conventional Commits
  5. Updated documentation: Update relevant docs for any API changes
  6. Tests: Add tests for new functionality
  7. Signed-off commits: Sign off your commits (git commit --signoff) to accept the Contributor License Agreement

items.title: Commit Message Format
items.text:
feat: add new my-source component

- Add MySource implementation with base.Source
- Register in factory
- Add unit tests for spec validation

Closes #123

items.title: General Principles
items.text:
• Follow Effective Go
  • Use idiomatic Go patterns
  • Keep code simple and readable
  • Comment only what's not obvious

items.title: Naming Conventions
items.text:
• Use camelCase for variables and functions
  • Use PascalCase for types and exported identifiers
  • Use snake_case for JSON tags
  • Type names should be nouns: UserService, not GetUser
  • Interface names should end with er: Logger, Writer

items.title: Formatting
items.text:
• Use gofmt for formatting
  • Line length: aim for 80-100 characters
  • Indent with tabs, not spaces
  • Group related imports and separate with blank lines

items.title: Structure
items.text:
• Keep functions short (aim for < 50 lines)
  • Group related functions together
  • Use receiver methods appropriately

items.title: Error Handling
items.text:
• Always check errors
  • Provide context in error messages
  • Use fmt.Errorf with %w for error wrapping
  • Return errors, don't panic (except in truly exceptional cases)
// Good
if err := doSomething(); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("failed to do something: %w", err)
}

// Bad
if err := doSomething(); err != nil {
    panic(err)
}

items.title: Unit Tests
items.text:
• Place test files next to the code they test (*_test.go)
  • Use table-driven tests for similar cases
  • Test both happy paths and error cases
func TestMyFunction(t *testing.T) {
    tests := []struct {
        name     string
        input    string
        expected string
        err      bool
    }{
        {"success", "valid", "result", false},
        {"error", "invalid", "", true},
    }

    for _, tt := range tests {
        t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {
            result, err := myFunction(tt.input)
            if (err != nil) != tt.err {
                t.Errorf("expected error: %v, got: %v", tt.err, err)
            }
            if !tt.err && result != tt.expected {
                t.Errorf("expected %q, got %q", tt.expected, result)
            }
        })
    }
}

items.title: End-to-End Tests
items.text:
internal/e2e tests complete pipelines without external dependencies: streams are built by the core from the real source and stage factories, OTLP data is sent over HTTP, and capturing sinks record exactly which records arrive where. They cover batching, splitting, cancelled requests, the status codes clients receive, and updates under load, and run with go test ./....

TestBrokerNATS in the same package runs pipelines against a NATS server in a container (see internal/testutil/natstest) and checks what actually ends up in JetStream: subjects, plain OTLP bodies without headers, and records with their resource and scope. It also sends data from the broker sink through the broker source, reads plain OTLP that another producer published, and checks partitioning, buffering and the answers clients get. TestBrokerKafka and TestBrokerAMQP do the same against Kafka and against ActiveMQ Artemis over AMQP 1.0 (see internal/testutil/kafkatest and amqptest). They are skipped without Docker or Podman; with Podman on macOS, set the variables described under Benchmarks.

When adding a stage or changing how events flow, add a case there that checks which records arrive in which sink.

items.title: Broker Drivers
items.text: A broker driver implements the contract in internal/adapters/broker and has to pass the conformance suite in broker/brokertest (brokertest.Run): publish and receive, acknowledge, retry after a delay, reject, a durable position across subscribers, cancellation, invalid destinations and the maximum message size. Run it against the broker in a container, as broker/nats does. Register the driver in broker/drivers, the only package that knows the concrete drivers; its options sit under its name in the component spec, which driver.Split takes apart. The broker sink only sees a driver's PublisherDriver side and the broker source its SubscriberDriver side, so neither can do the other's job. Unit tests of the broker source and sink inject the in-memory driver of brokertest through NewWithDrivers (see their export_test.go) and need no container.

items.title: Stage Drivers
items.text:
The filter and validation stages are concepts whose rules come from a driver, as the broker components' messaging does: the spec names it in driver and holds its options under its name, e.g. driver: cel and cel: {...}. driver.Split takes the spec apart, so the stage parses only its own fields (on_mismatch for validation) and the driver only its options.

The stage owns what every driver shares: walking the records and pruning what becomes empty (filter), dropping or rejecting (validation), and turning a failing rule into a rejection. A driver only compiles its options into rules:

  • filter: filter.Driver returns filter.Rules, whose Predicates give a predicate per signal for one event. A nil predicate keeps all records of its signal
  • validation: validation.Driver returns validation.Rules, which decide per signal whether the whole signal matches. A signal without a rule matches

Each stage is laid out like the broker components: the contract package (rules, persist), one package per driver (cel, sqlite) that knows only the contract, and a drivers package, the only one that knows the concrete drivers. The stage creates its drivers factory itself in New; stage/factory.go knows no drivers. To add a driver, e.g. OTTL, create stage/filter/ottl next to stage/filter/cel with a Name and a Driver and register it in stage/filter/drivers. Test it through the stage as filter/cel does, so the rules are checked with the stage's pruning and rejection. The depguard rules in .golangci.yml enforce the layout: factories import no drivers, and only a drivers package imports concrete drivers (tests excepted).

items.title: Kubernetes Operator Tests
items.text: The TestOperator* tests in internal/adapters/k8scrd run the operator against a real kube-apiserver and etcd from envtest, one per test. They check which Stream resources an instance runs with --watch-namespace and --engine, and that the generated RBAC role works with a namespaced RoleBinding. They are skipped unless KUBEBUILDER_ASSETS is set; task test:envtest downloads the binaries with setup-envtest and sets it.

items.title: Integration Tests
items.text:
• Use test containers for external dependencies (NATS, etc.), see internal/testutil/natstest
  • Clean up resources after tests

items.title: Benchmarks
items.text:
Benchmarks cover the per-event hot path:

Benchmark Package Measures BenchmarkNotifySubscribers source/base, stage/base Fan-out cost per event and child BenchmarkPipeline core A full stream with real stages, in records/s BenchmarkCELValidator stage/validation/cel Expression evaluation per payload size BenchmarkCELFilter stage/filter/cel Per-record filtering for different keep ratios BenchmarkFilter core/domain The record filtering helpers without CEL BenchmarkNotify sink/broker Grouping and publishing to NATS through the NATS driver (container) BenchmarkConsume source/broker Receiving, decoding and acknowledging from NATS through the NATS driver (container) BenchmarkBatch stage/batch Batch overhead and merging with concurrent callers BenchmarkHandleLogs source/otlp Reading and decoding OTLP requests BenchmarkOTLPDataRoundTrip core/domain Serializing events as OTLP data, as the broker sink and source do BenchmarkScenario scenario Complete pipelines end to end: throughput, CPU per record, latency (container) BenchmarkStreams scenario Cost of idle streams for 10 to 1,000 streams per instance: build time, heap, goroutines, NATS connections and requests of the broker sources and sinks, idle CPU (container; each case takes about 20 seconds, run it with -benchtime 1x)

BENCHMARK.md presents these results. After performance-relevant changes, regenerate it with task bench:report (see the page for details); add new scenarios to internal/scenario and new components to the lists in tools/benchreport.

Benchmarks marked "container" start a NATS server with Testcontainers via internal/testutil/natstest. They need Docker or Podman and are skipped if neither is running. With Podman, Testcontainers needs the socket of the Podman service; the tasks set it up from podman info when Podman is installed. To run go test directly, set the same:

export TESTCONTAINERS_DOCKER_SOCKET_OVERRIDE=$(podman info --format '{{.Host.RemoteSocket.Path}}')
export TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_CONTAINER_PRIVILEGED=true
# Podman on Linux only, not in a Podman machine on macOS or Windows:
export DOCKER_HOST=unix://$TESTCONTAINERS_DOCKER_SOCKET_OVERRIDE

Build payloads with internal/testutil/otlpgen and use otlpgen.Shapes so results are comparable across benchmarks. Use b.Loop(), call b.ReportAllocs(), and report records/s for payload-dependent benchmarks.

Compare a change against main with benchstat:

git switch main && task bench COUNT=10 > old.txt
git switch my-branch && task bench COUNT=10 > new.txt
task bench:compare OLD=old.txt NEW=new.txt

-p 1 runs one package at a time. Without it, go test benchmarks several packages in parallel, which then compete for CPU and distort each other's results. Other load on the machine, like a container VM that is just starting, has the same effect; check the spread between runs before trusting a result.

items.text:
• Document exported types, functions, and methods
  • Use complete sentences for doc comments
  • Include examples where helpful
// User represents a system user.
// It contains basic user information and access permissions.
type User struct {
    Name string
    Age  int

// Validate checks if the user data is valid.
// Returns an error if any field is invalid.

items.title: Architecture Decisions
items.text: Decisions that are hard to reverse, change a contract (configuration, API, delivery semantics, metrics) or turn down an obvious alternative are recorded in docs/adr/. A pull request that makes such a decision adds a record, or a new one that supersedes an old one; see Writing a Record.

items.title: API Documentation
items.text:
• The swagger file is automatically generated from protobuf definitions
  • No manual updates needed when changing API endpoints

items.title: Component Documentation
items.text:
When adding new components:

  1. Add a section to COMPONENTS.md, headed ### <Name> Source, ### <Name> Stage or ### <Name> Sink under its group, and a linked row to the group's table of available components
  2. Include:
  3. Configuration options
  4. Usage examples
  5. Behavior description
  6. Error cases
  7. The documentation site gives every component a page of its own, derived from that heading, e.g. ### Value Map Stage becomes components/stages/value-map.md. Add it to the navigation in docs/zensical.toml; docs/generate.py fails until it is there
  8. If the component has a benchmark, add its rows to tools/benchreport with a section name, and a #### Performance subsection with the markers <!-- BEGIN benchreport:component:<name> --> and <!-- END benchreport:component:<name> -->, which benchreport fills from the same run as BENCHMARK.md. Write tips in that subsection in relative terms, without absolute numbers, which depend on the machine

items.title: Checks on Pull Requests
items.text:
The CI workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs on GitHub-hosted runners (ubuntu-latest) for every pull request and every push to main, as five parallel jobs: task ci:lint runs golangci-lint in the version pinned in Taskfile.yml and govulncheck, task ci:test the unit and end-to-end tests, task ci:containers the tests of the NATS, Kafka and AMQP broker packages and the end-to-end broker tests against containers, which take the longest, task ci:envtest the operator tests against kube-apiserver and etcd from setup-envtest, and task ci:chart checks the Helm chart. That job regenerates the CRDs and roles with controller-gen and fails if they differ from the ones committed in manifests/ and charts/tram, then runs task chart:lint: helm lint --strict, and the chart rendered with the default and other values validated against the Kubernetes schemas with kubeconform.

Each job caches the Go modules and builds, and the lint job golangci-lint's results, under a key of its own. Pushes to main save a new cache per run; pull requests and the release workflow only restore the latest one, so they stay fast without filling the cache storage.

The actions the workflows use are pinned to the commit of a release, with the version in a comment; update both together.

Upgrade test. Pull requests that change the operator, the chart, the manifests, the image or the test itself also run .github/workflows/upgrade.yml. In a kind cluster, it installs the latest release, creates an Engine with storage whose streams buffer records for a receiver that does not exist yet, upgrades to the chart and image of the pull request, and checks that the Engine runs the new image, its streams are mounted again, the CRDs match the repository, and every buffered record reaches the receiver once it exists. The release workflow runs it from the previous release before it publishes. Run it locally with task test:upgrade; the steps are in test/upgrade/run.sh.

items.title: Releases
items.text:
A release is a version tag on main. The release workflow (.github/workflows/release.yml) refuses tags that are not on main, runs the same lint, test, containers and chart jobs and the upgrade test from the previous release, and then builds the image with Docker Buildx for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 and pushes it to ghcr.io/go-tram/tram as the version without the leading v (e.g. 0.1.0) and as latest. Then it publishes the Helm chart charts/tram to oci://ghcr.io/go-tram/charts/tram with that version as chart and app version, renders manifests/ with the image of that version into tram.yaml, and attaches both to the GitHub Release of the tag, which it creates if it does not exist. The image gets an SBOM and a provenance attestation, and image and chart are signed with cosign, keyless through the workflow's GitHub OIDC token; SECURITY.md shows how to verify them. It also pushes charts/artifacthub-repo.yml as the tag artifacthub.io of the chart's repository, from which Artifact Hub reads the repository ID and owners. In the repository the chart keeps the version 0.0.0 and the manifests the image tag latest; do not bump them.

Tag releases with the release tasks rather than by hand. They use svu to compute the version from the existing tags, check that you are on main, that it matches origin/main and has no uncommitted changes, run task check, and then create and push the annotated tag:

task release:next    # from the Conventional Commits since the last tag: breaking → major, feat → minor, others → patch
task release:patch   # v0.1.0 → v0.1.1
task release:minor   # v0.1.0 → v0.2.0
task release:major   # v0.1.0 → v1.0.0

A breaking change is a pull request title with ! before the colon, e.g. feat(api)!: remove the v1alpha1 Stream API, or a BREAKING CHANGE: line in its description, which becomes the body of the squashed commit. While the version is 0.x, release:next bumps the minor version for a breaking change instead of the major one, so v1.0.0 is only tagged on purpose, with release:major.

items.title: Architecture Decisions
items.text:
This directory records the decisions that shape TRAM, as Architecture Decision Records (ADRs): what was decided, why, and what follows from it. The documentation describes how TRAM behaves; the records explain why it behaves that way and which alternatives were turned down, so a later change can tell a deliberate trade-off from an oversight.

ADR Decision Status 0001 Record architecture decisions Accepted 0002 OTLP as the data model of the core Accepted 0003 Ports and adapters Accepted 0004 Components as concept and driver Accepted 0005 Events are shared and read-only Accepted 0006 At-least-once delivery without deduplication Accepted 0007 Synchronous delivery and backpressure Accepted 0008 Requests are accepted or refused as a whole Accepted 0009 No authentication or authorization in TRAM Accepted 0010 One set of streams, the last write wins Superseded by 0018 0011 Transform stage with a CEL driver, attributes only Accepted 0012 Object storage sink with S3 as its first driver Accepted, not built 0013 A driver for value_map only when needed Proposed 0014 Releases from Conventional Commits Accepted 0015 Streams keep nothing on disk; buffers connect two streams Accepted 0016 Limit the request size at the source, decompressed Accepted 0017 Operations on different streams run in parallel Accepted 0018 Stream resources own their streams Accepted

items.title: Writing a Record
items.text:
Add a decision that is hard to reverse, changes a contract (configuration, API, delivery semantics, metrics) or turns down an obvious alternative. Smaller choices belong in the pull request.

  • Copy the structure of an existing record into NNNN-short-title.md, with the next free number, and add it to the table above and to the navigation in docs/zensical.toml
  • Status: Proposed while it is discussed, Accepted once decided (Accepted, not built until it is implemented), Superseded by NNNN when a later record replaces it. Records are not deleted or rewritten; a changed decision gets a new record
  • Date: when the decision was made. Records 0002 to 0015 were written down on 2026-11-23 for decisions made before; their dates are those of the decision where it is known
  • Keep them short: context, decision, consequences, and the alternatives that were turned down

items.title: 0001: Record Architecture Decisions
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-23

items.title: Context
items.text: TRAM has many contracts: configuration fields, the API, delivery semantics, status codes, metric names. The reasons behind them were spread over pull request descriptions and discussions, and an external architecture review asked for a place that keeps them. More people now work on TRAM, and they need to tell deliberate trade-offs from gaps.

items.title: Decision
items.text: Decisions are recorded as Architecture Decision Records in docs/adr/, one Markdown file each, numbered, with status, date, context, decision and consequences. They are part of the documentation site under Development → Decisions.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• A pull request that makes such a decision adds or supersedes a record
  • Records describe why; the README and COMPONENTS.md stay the reference for how TRAM behaves, and records link there instead of repeating it

items.title: 0002: OTLP as the Data Model of the Core
items.text: • Status: Accepted
path: 0002: OTLP as the Data Model of the Core

items.title: Context
items.text: TRAM moves telemetry between OpenTelemetry clients, brokers and backends. A pipeline can work on its own internal format and convert at the edges, like the OpenTelemetry Collector's pdata, or on the wire format itself.
path: 0002: OTLP as the Data Model of the Core

items.title: Decision
items.text: The core works on the OTLP protobuf types directly: an event holds LogsData, MetricsData or TracesData, and the domain package also encodes and decodes them (MarshalOTLPPayloads, UnmarshalOTLPData). There is no internal data model of TRAM's own. The OTLP source has no driver, since OTLP is the technology it serves; HTTP and gRPC are its ports.
path: 0002: OTLP as the Data Model of the Core

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• No conversion between sources, stages and sinks: what a client sent is what a sink sends on, and a broker between two streams carries plain OTLP
  • CEL expressions see the OTLP structure, with the field names users know from the specification
  • Another data format, e.g. a non-OTLP log format, cannot be plugged in as an adapter; it would have to be converted to OTLP at a source. That is accepted: TRAM is an OTLP pipeline
  • New OTLP fields arrive with the protobuf module; copies of events have to keep them, which TestCopiesKeepEveryField checks
path: 0002: OTLP as the Data Model of the Core

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: • An internal model (like pdata): decouples the core from the wire format, at the cost of a conversion on every hop and a second model to learn. Not needed while TRAM only speaks OTLP
path: 0002: OTLP as the Data Model of the Core

items.title: 0003: Ports and Adapters
items.text: • Status: Accepted

items.title: Context
items.text: TRAM is configured from three places (API, files, Kubernetes resources) and talks to many technologies (NATS, Kafka, AMQP, SQLite, KMS). The stream logic should not depend on any of them.

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The code follows a ports-and-adapters structure:

  • internal/core/domain: events, specs and the contracts of components, depending only on the OTLP protobufs and the standard library
  • internal/ports: the interfaces the core offers and needs
  • internal/core: builds and runs streams
  • internal/adapters: everything that touches the outside, i.e. the API, file sync, operator, sources, stages, sinks and their drivers

Dependencies point inwards: adapters import the core and the domain, never the other way around. Components implement small interfaces (Observer, Subscriber, Stoppable, …) instead of one large one.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• A new configuration source or component is a new adapter; the core does not change
  • Tests of the core use fake sources and sinks; tests of adapters use the real core

items.title: 0004: Components as Concept and Driver
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-18

items.title: Context
items.text: Several components do the same thing with different technologies: a broker sink publishes to NATS, Kafka or AMQP; encryption uses local keys or a KMS; validation uses CEL or rules. One component type per technology would repeat the shared behavior (destinations, batching, metrics, error handling) and its configuration in each.

items.title: Decision
items.text:
A component is a concept, and the technology it uses is its driver:

  • The component's spec has a driver field and the options of the driver under a field named after it, e.g. {"driver": "nats", "nats": {"url": …}}
  • Fields shared by all drivers stay at the component level; the driver interface is small and holds only what differs
  • driver always means the technology the component talks to or evaluates with. Other axes get their own field, e.g. the format of the planned object storage sink (0012)
  • Components that are their technology, like the OTLP source and sink, have no driver

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• A new technology is a new driver, with the shared behavior, configuration and tests of its component for free
  • Adding a driver to a component that has none is a breaking change of its configuration, see 0013

items.title: 0005: Events Are Shared and Read-Only
items.text: • Status: Accepted

items.title: Context
items.text: A stream is a tree: after a stage, every branch receives the event, concurrently. Copying the event for every branch costs memory and time in proportion to its size; sharing it is free, but a branch that changes it would change it for the others while they read it.

items.title: Decision
items.text: An event is passed by reference to all branches and is read-only for every subscriber. A stage that changes data forwards a copy and leaves the event it received as it is. Copies are shallow where possible: a stage copies only the parts it changes and shares the rest (copy on write), e.g. the transform stage copies a resource only when a statement changes it.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Fan-out costs nothing per branch. A stage that writes to a shared event is a data race, which the tests, run with -race, catch
  • A partial copy has to keep every field of the OTLP types it copies; TestCopiesKeepEveryField fails when a new protobuf field is not copied

items.title: 0006: At-Least-Once Delivery Without Deduplication
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07

items.title: Context
items.text: Data can be lost or duplicated between a client and a sink: a sink fails after others accepted the data, a broker redelivers a message, an acknowledgement gets lost. Exactly-once would need deduplication by ID across restarts and instances, which OTLP data does not provide.

items.title: Decision
items.text: Delivery is at-least-once: TRAM answers a request with success only once all sinks accepted the data, and otherwise answers so that the client retries. It does not deduplicate. Duplicates are left to the destination, which can deduplicate where it matters.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• A sink can receive the same data more than once, e.g. after a 503 that the client retries although some sinks had accepted the data; COMPONENTS.md documents the cases under Stream Behavior
  • At-least-once holds only as far as the sender retries; agents and SDKs need retries enabled

items.title: 0007: Synchronous Delivery and Backpressure
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-03

items.title: Context
items.text: A pipeline can acknowledge data when it arrives and deliver it later from a queue, or acknowledge it only once it is delivered. The first decouples senders from slow sinks, but data in the queue is lost when the process dies, and the sender cannot tell.

items.title: Decision
items.text: TRAM acknowledges a request only after the stream delivered it. A batch stage holds every request until its batch is delivered, so a sender waits up to the batch's timeout. Slow or failing sinks slow down senders instead of filling a queue. Where data has to survive a sink's outage, a buffer sink or a broker between streams is configured explicitly, and the acknowledgement then means "stored".

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Senders feel backpressure: with a batch stage, a sender that sends one request at a time gets one request through per batch timeout; concurrency on the sender side raises throughput
  • delivery_timeout, batch timeouts and the senders' timeouts have to fit together, see Hold Times in COMPONENTS.md
  • Nothing is acknowledged that TRAM could still lose in memory

items.title: 0008: Requests Are Accepted or Refused as a Whole
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
path: 0008: Requests Are Accepted or Refused as a Whole

items.title: Context
items.text: OTLP clients retry only some responses (HTTP 429, 502, 503, 504; gRPC Unavailable and a few others) and drop data on the rest. OTLP also allows partial success. A wrong choice either loses data that would have succeeded on a retry, or makes clients retry forever what will never succeed.
path: 0008: Requests Are Accepted or Refused as a Whole

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• A request becomes one event, which is never split, and it is accepted or refused as a whole; partial success is not used
  • A response is retriable only if the client did nothing wrong: 503 (Unavailable with RetryInfo) when delivery failed or took longer than delivery_timeout. Data that cannot be read or that a stage or sink rejects gets 422 (InvalidArgument), an unsupported content type 415, a body above the size limit 413 (ResourceExhausted)
  • A rejection is 422 wherever it comes from, including a sink whose destination refuses the data permanently because of its own configuration. That is documented as a caveat rather than turned into a retriable status
path: 0008: Requests Are Accepted or Refused as a Whole

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Clients never retry data that cannot succeed, and retry everything else
  • One bad record refuses its whole request, also in a batch: validate before a batch stage so one sender's bad request does not fail a batch shared with others
path: 0008: Requests Are Accepted or Refused as a Whole

items.title: 0009: No Authentication or Authorization in TRAM
items.text: • Status: Accepted
path: 0009: No Authentication or Authorization in TRAM

items.title: Context
items.text: TRAM opens ports, receives data and sends it anywhere a stream says. Authentication, TLS and tenant identity could be built into TRAM, but every deployment already has a way to do them, e.g. an ingress, a service mesh or network policies, and they differ between deployments.
path: 0009: No Authentication or Authorization in TRAM

items.title: Decision
items.text: TRAM has no authentication or authorization of its own, and the OTLP source serves without TLS. They are the job of the infrastructure in front of TRAM. Access to a configuration source (API, configuration directory, Stream resources) is access to the TRAM process. What a proxy knows about a request, e.g. the tenant, reaches the data through header_attributes: the header decides the attribute, and a value the client set itself is replaced.
path: 0009: No Authentication or Authorization in TRAM

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• TRAM has to be deployed behind something that authenticates, and only that may reach its ports; the README's Security section lists what to restrict
  • Granting create on Stream resources is as powerful as access to the TRAM deployment
  • Revisit before 1.0 whether TLS on the OTLP source or authentication of the API belongs into TRAM as a generic capability
path: 0009: No Authentication or Authorization in TRAM

items.title: 0010: One Set of Streams, the Last Write Wins
items.text: • Status: Superseded by 0018
path: 0010: One Set of Streams, the Last Write Wins

items.title: Context
items.text: Streams can come from the API, from files (file sync) and from Stream resources (operator), also at the same time. Each source could own its streams, with TRAM refusing changes from others, or all could write to one shared state.
path: 0010: One Set of Streams, the Last Write Wins

items.title: Decision
items.text: The core holds one set of streams, and every source writes to it through the same operations. A stream has no owner: the last write decides what runs. The file sync writes changes of the other sources back to files, so the files mirror what runs. The operator applies a resource when it changes and when the instance starts, and does not write back. The README's Conflicts Between Configuration Sources describes what follows for each combination.
path: 0010: One Set of Streams, the Last Write Wins

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• The sources stay simple and independent, and the API can always read what runs
  • A change from another source to a stream of a Stream resource lasts until the resource changes or the instance restarts. Operators are told to give every stream one owning source
  • Ownership could be enforced later, e.g. by refusing API changes to streams of resources, without changing the data model
path: 0010: One Set of Streams, the Last Write Wins

items.title: Alternatives
items.text:
• Ownership per stream: clear, but needs an owner field in every stream, rules for taking a stream over, and errors for users who only wanted to try a change through the API
  • The operator writes back to resources: makes Kubernetes the single source, but gives TRAM write access to resources and creates update loops between instances
path: 0010: One Set of Streams, the Last Write Wins

items.title: 0011: Transform Stage With a CEL Driver, Attributes Only
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-22
path: 0011: Transform Stage With a CEL Driver, Attributes Only

items.title: Context
items.text: Users need to change data in a stream: set, delete or rename attributes, truncate values. value_map already maps values through tables; the encryption stage covers redaction.
path: 0011: Transform Stage With a CEL Driver, Attributes Only

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• A transform stage, as concept and driver (0004): driver: cel first, with its statements under cel. An ottl driver may follow, with OTTL's own statements; only stage-level fields are shared between drivers
  • Version 1 changes attributes of records, resources and scopes: set, delete, rename, truncate, each with an optional when. Not the log body or severity, no hashing, no parsing of bodies. The target paths form a grammar, so adding body or severity_* later is not a breaking change
  • on_error decides what a failing statement does: skip (the default: skip the statement, keep the entry, count it), reject (422) or drop
  • Boundary to value_map: transform is logic over an entry, value_map is data from tables. Transform has no lookup function, value_map no expressions; a stream chains both
  • Everything compiles when the stream is created, so a dry run reports errors
path: 0011: Transform Stage With a CEL Driver, Attributes Only

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Copies follow 0005: only changed parts are copied
  • Body and severity changes, OTTL and hashing are later additions, not part of v1
path: 0011: Transform Stage With a CEL Driver, Attributes Only

items.title: 0012: Object Storage Sink With S3 as Its First Driver
items.text:
• Status: Accepted, not built
  • Date: 2026-11-22
path: 0012: Object Storage Sink With S3 as Its First Driver

items.title: Context
items.text: Data should be archived in object storage, e.g. for long retention or analysis. Most providers speak the S3 API (AWS, STACKIT, MinIO, Ceph, R2); the format of the objects is a choice of its own (OTLP protobuf or JSON, Parquet, plain log bodies).
path: 0012: Object Storage Sink With S3 as Its First Driver

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• A sink type: object_storage, with the storage API as its driver (0004): s3 first, then file for local directories and tests; others only on demand. The driver interface stays small: put an object with metadata, its size limit, checking a key, closing
  • The format is a separate field, format, with its options under its own name (otlp_proto, otlp_json, parquet, body). Encoders live in their own package, so other sinks can use them
  • The sink, not the driver, collects events into objects by size and age, builds keys from a template, encodes and compresses, and acknowledges after the upload (at-least-once, 0006)
  • Order: s3 with otlp_proto, then Parquet for logs and traces, then metrics
path: 0012: Object Storage Sink With S3 as Its First Driver

items.title: Open
items.text: • Whether the sink collects into objects itself or relies on a batch stage before it; the sink collecting itself is preferred
path: 0012: Object Storage Sink With S3 as Its First Driver

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: • Format as the driver: turned down, since driver means the technology talked to everywhere else, and format and storage vary independently
path: 0012: Object Storage Sink With S3 as Its First Driver

items.title: 0013: A Driver for value_map Only When Needed
items.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Date: 2026-11-23
path: 0013: A Driver for value_map Only When Needed

items.title: Context
items.text: value_map maps attribute values through a table in its spec, from config maps or from secrets. Mappings that change often, e.g. tenant to router, could come from an external store such as Redis.
path: 0013: A Driver for value_map Only When Needed

items.title: Decision
items.text: value_map does not get a driver field now. When an external store is needed, it becomes concept and driver (0004): driver: table for today's tables, driver: redis with its options. The stage-level fields (source_attr, target_attr, default, level, metrics) stay. The change is breaking, since driver becomes required, which before 1.0 is a minor version.
path: 0013: A Driver for value_map Only When Needed

items.title: Open Before a Redis Driver
items.text:
1. Speed: a lookup over the network per record would cost far more than today's ~125 ns; it needs a cache with a TTL and one batched lookup per event
  2. Store unavailable: set default, or answer 503 so senders retry; a stage-level field such as on_unavailable
  3. Consistency: a changed mapping applies only after the cache TTL, so data briefly follows the old one
path: 0013: A Driver for value_map Only When Needed

items.title: 0014: Releases From Conventional Commits
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-22

items.title: Context
items.text: Releases need a version that says what changed, notes for users, and artifacts that users can verify.

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• Pull requests are squash-merged, and their titles follow Conventional Commits, checked in CI; the title becomes the commit on main
  • Versions are computed from these commits with svu (next --always --v0): before 1.0, a breaking change raises the minor version and anything else the patch version
  • git-cliff writes the release notes from the same commits, for the GitHub Release and the Releases page of the documentation
  • Commits are signed. Release images and charts are signed with cosign (keyless) and carry an SBOM and a provenance attestation

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• A pull request title is part of the changelog and decides the version, so it has to describe the change for users
  • Users can verify that an image or chart was built by the release workflow from a tag

items.title: 0015: Streams Keep Nothing on Disk; Buffers Connect Two Streams
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-21
path: 0015: Streams Keep Nothing on Disk; Buffers Connect Two Streams

items.title: Context
items.text: Some setups need to answer clients before the destination has the data, e.g. to ride out an outage of the destination, and some have no broker such as NATS to put in between. A stream could get a write-ahead log of its own, e.g. as a stage that persists events before passing them on.
path: 0015: Streams Keep Nothing on Disk; Buffers Connect Two Streams

items.title: Decision
items.text: A stream processes events only in memory and keeps nothing on disk (0007). Writing ahead is built from two streams and a queue between them: a buffer sink stores events in a queue on the instance's disk (driver sqlite), and a buffer source in another stream reads and delivers them, retrying until the queue's max_age. The queue name connects the two. The buffer is a broker embedded in the instance, and its source and sink behave like the broker source and sink.
path: 0015: Streams Keep Nothing on Disk; Buffers Connect Two Streams

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Streams stay synchronous and stateless; whether and where data is persisted is visible in the configuration, not hidden in a stage
  • The same pattern works with a real broker between the streams, so moving from a local buffer to NATS, Kafka or AMQP changes components, not the design
  • A local queue is one copy on one instance: losing the disk loses the data, another instance cannot deliver its backlog, and scaling down needs the queue drained first, which the manager does for Engines with drain Jobs. Where that is not acceptable, a replicated broker between the streams is the choice
  • No write-ahead logic per stage, branch or sink to build and test
path: 0015: Streams Keep Nothing on Disk; Buffers Connect Two Streams

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: • A write-ahead log inside a stream, e.g. a WAL stage: would persist data in the middle of a synchronous pipeline, need tracking per branch for fan-out, and duplicate what a queue between streams already does
path: 0015: Streams Keep Nothing on Disk; Buffers Connect Two Streams

items.title: 0016: Limit the Request Size at the Source, Decompressed
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-23
path: 0016: Limit the Request Size at the Source, Decompressed

items.title: Context
items.text: Events are never split (0008). A broker sink rejects an event with a message larger than the broker accepts, e.g. NATS' max_payload, but only after it has sent the event's other messages; a buffer sink rejects an event above its max_bytes. A large request thus could be delivered in part and then refused.
path: 0016: Limit the Request Size at the Source, Decompressed

items.title: Decision
items.text: The OTLP source limits the size of a request with max_request_bytes (20 MiB by default, which was the fixed limit before) and refuses larger requests with 413 (ResourceExhausted over gRPC) before decoding them. The limit applies to the body as sent and after decompression; what counts is the decompressed size, since that is what the stream and the limits after it see, and it guards against compression bombs. The size is not limited by a separate stage, since a stage only sees the decoded event, after the cost was paid.
path: 0016: Limit the Request Size at the Source, Decompressed

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Set max_request_bytes and a batch stage's max_bytes below the smallest limit downstream, so no message is too large there
  • A proxy in front of TRAM sees only the compressed size; its limit protects the proxy, and TRAM's the pipeline
path: 0016: Limit the Request Size at the Source, Decompressed

items.title: 0017: Operations on Different Streams Run in Parallel
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-24
path: 0017: Operations on Different Streams Run in Parallel

items.title: Context
items.text: The core guarded all streams with one lock, held while a stream was built or stopped and while watchers were notified. Building a stream can take long, e.g. while its sinks connect to a broker, and stopping one waits for the deliveries in progress. One slow stream held up every other change, reads through the API, the operator and the file sync. An instance loaded its streams one after the other, both from files and from Stream resources, and stopped them one after the other on shutdown.
path: 0017: Operations on Different Streams Run in Parallel

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• A lock per stream name. Creating, updating, deleting, restarting and planning a stream hold the lock of its name for the whole operation and read the running stream only once they hold it. Operations on one name run one after the other; those on different names run in parallel. The lock belongs to the name, not to the running stream: a stream is replaced on every update, and a new name has no stream yet to lock
  • A short lock for the core's state. It guards the map of streams, the watchers and whether the core is closed, and is never held while a stream is built or stopped, nor while watchers are notified
  • A new stream is listed once its watchers know it. GetStream and GetStreams show a new stream only after every watcher received its event. The file sync relies on it: it deletes listed streams without a file, and writes the file when it receives the event
  • Close refuses new operations, waits for those in progress, stops all streams in parallel, and gives up waiting when its context ends; tram server allows 25 seconds
  • Loading in parallel. The file sync applies and deletes up to 8 streams at once, and the operator reconciles up to 8 Stream resources at once
path: 0017: Operations on Different Streams Run in Parallel

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• An instance with many streams starts and stops faster, as much as the streams take long to connect, and a new replica runs its streams sooner
  • A slow or failing stream no longer holds up the others or the API
  • Changes to one stream from several sources still apply one after the other, and the last one wins (0010)
  • A watcher that is slow to receive events holds up the operations on that stream, not the core
  • Connections to brokers are opened by up to 8 streams at once, not all of them: the bound keeps a start from flooding a broker or the Kubernetes API
path: 0017: Operations on Different Streams Run in Parallel

items.title: Alternatives
items.text:
• A lock per running stream: turned down, since an update replaces the stream: an operation waiting for the lock of the old one would continue with a stream that is gone, and two creations of a new name would find nothing to lock
  • No bound on parallel loading: turned down, since hundreds of streams would connect to their brokers, and read their secrets from the Kubernetes API, at the same moment
path: 0017: Operations on Different Streams Run in Parallel

items.title: 0018: Stream Resources Own Their Streams
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-24
  • Supersedes: 0010

items.title: Context
items.text: Under 0010, a stream belonged to no source and the last write won. The operator applied a Stream resource only when it changed and when the instance started, so a change through the API or the file sync to the stream of a resource lasted until then, possibly for weeks, and differed between the instances of an Engine. A deleted file stopped the stream the same way. Kubernetes users expect a resource to describe what runs.

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• A Stream resource owns the stream of its name, <namespace>.<name>, on every instance that runs it. The operator watches the changes of the core, the same way the file sync does, and reconciles the resource of every changed or deleted stream; the reconcile applies the resource again if the stream differs from it, or starts it again if it was deleted
  • The operator reconciles only streams of resources it runs: resources in its cache, i.e. in a watched namespace and, with an engine, labeled for it, whose spec.engineRefs name the engine. A stream under a name like <namespace>.<name> without such a resource is left alone, since the reconcile of a missing resource would delete it
  • Changes are undone, not refused: the API and the file sync still accept them, and the operator applies the resource right after. The core keeps no owner per stream
  • The operator receives the changes of the core without waiting for its controller, which starts later; the core is never held up by the operator
  • Streams that no resource owns keep the rule of 0010: the last write wins

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• What runs matches the resources, on every instance, within a moment of a change elsewhere
  • A change to the stream of a resource through the API or a file has an effect only for that moment, e.g. it may restart the stream's source once
  • With file sync, the file of a stream of a resource follows the resource again after an edit
  • The operator's own changes reach it as well; their reconciles find the stream as the resource describes it and change nothing
  • tram drain runs no API or file sync and does not watch the core

items.title: Alternatives
items.text:
• Refuse changes to streams of resources in the API and the file sync: clearer for the user, but the core would need an owner per stream and every source would need to know about the operator. Can be added later, on top of this
  • Write changes back to the resources: gives TRAM write access to the resources and lets instances overwrite each other

items.title: API Endpoints
items.text:
The TRAM service provides the following HTTP endpoints:

Method Endpoint Description GET /v1/streams List all streams, ordered by name PUT /v1/streams/{name} Create or update a stream GET /v1/streams/{name} Get a stream configuration DELETE /v1/streams/{name} Delete a stream GET /metrics Metrics of TRAM in the Prometheus format, see Metrics

The stream name is taken from the URL; a name in the request body is replaced by it.

items.title: Create a Pipeline with Stages
items.text:
This example adds a noop stage between the source and sinks:

curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/processing-pipeline \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "stream": {
      "name": "processing-pipeline",
      "source": {
        "name": "events-source",
        "type": "generator",
        "spec": {
          "interval": "1s"
        }
      },
      "stages": [
        {
          "name": "passthrough",
          "type": "noop",
          "from": "events-source"
        }
      ],
      "sinks": [
        {
          "name": "console",
          "type": "debug",
          "from": "passthrough"
        }
      ]
    }
  }'

items.title: Get Stream Configuration
items.text: curl http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/my-pipeline

items.title: Delete a Stream
items.text: curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/my-pipeline

items.title: Installation
items.text:
git clone https://github.com/go-tram/tram.git tram
cd tram
go build -o tram ./cmd/tram

Or build a container image with Docker or Podman: task image:build (with Task) or docker build -t tram:dev .. Run task to see all development tasks, e.g. for tests and benchmarks; CONTRIBUTING.md explains them.

items.title: Run
items.text:
./tram server

The container image starts the server with both APIs listening on all interfaces of the container: docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -p 50051:50051 tram:dev.

By default the HTTP API listens on localhost:8080 and the gRPC API on localhost:50051. --log-level sets the log level (debug, info, warn or error; default info). See ./tram server --help for all flags.

items.title: Create a First Stream
items.text:
Create a stream whose generator source emits an event every 5 seconds and whose debug sink logs it to stdout:

curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/my-pipeline \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "stream": {
      "name": "my-pipeline",
      "source": {
        "name": "event-generator",
        "type": "generator",
        "spec": {
          "interval": "5s"
        }
      },
      "sinks": [
        {
          "name": "console",
          "type": "debug",
          "from": "event-generator"
        }
      ]
    }
  }'

More examples are under Example API Usage.

items.title: Security
items.text:
TRAM has no authentication or authorization of its own. Whoever can create a stream decides which ports TRAM opens and where it sends data, so treat access to every configuration source like access to the TRAM process:

  • API: the gRPC and HTTP APIs accept every request. They listen on localhost by default; if you bind them to other interfaces with --grpc-endpoint and --http-endpoint, restrict access, e.g. with a network policy or an authenticating proxy in front
  • Profiling: --pprof-endpoint serves the Go profiles under /debug/pprof/ on their own endpoint, without authentication; it is off by default. Profiles reveal internals such as stack traces and command-line arguments, so bind it to localhost or a port that is not exposed, and reach it with kubectl port-forward. It also turns on mutex and block profiling, which costs a little on contended locks
  • OTLP source: listens on the configured port on all network interfaces, without TLS or authentication. Anyone who can reach the port can send data into the stream. Restrict it on the network level, or terminate TLS and authenticate in a proxy in front of it
  • Sinks: an OTLP sink sends data to any URL in its spec, and insecure: true turns off certificate checks. Keep credentials in sink specs, e.g. in headers or NATS URLs, out of version control; the file sync writes new files readable only by their owner
  • Kubernetes operator: watches Stream resources in all namespaces unless --watch-namespace is set, so everyone allowed to create a Stream in a watched namespace can open ports on the TRAM pod and send data anywhere TRAM can reach. A Stream can also refer to secrets and config maps in its namespace, which TRAM reads and passes to the stream, so its author can send their values anywhere. Grant create on streams.io.tram.core only to users you would also trust with the TRAM deployment and with the secrets and config maps of that namespace. spec.engineRefs is no access control either: anyone who can create a Stream in an Engine's namespace can run it on that Engine

items.title: Sending Data to TRAM
items.text:
TRAM receives data; it does not collect it. Clients push OTLP over HTTP or gRPC to an OTLP Source, or TRAM reads from a broker or a buffer. There is no source that scrapes Prometheus endpoints or tails log files, so whatever cannot send OTLP itself needs an agent that collects its data and sends it on:

flowchart LR
    sdk["App with an OpenTelemetry SDK"] -- "OTLP/HTTP or gRPC" --> tram(["TRAM<br/>OTLP source"])
    scrape["App with /metrics"] -. scraped by .-> agent["Agent: OpenTelemetry Collector,<br/>Grafana Alloy or Fluent Bit"]
    files["Log files of the node"] -. read by .-> agent
    agent -- "OTLP/HTTP or gRPC" --> tram
    producer["Producer"] -- "OTLP protobuf messages" --> broker[("NATS, Kafka or AMQP")]
    broker --> tram2(["TRAM<br/>broker source"])
Pattern How When SDK The application exports OTLP itself, e.g. with OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://<tram>:4317 over gRPC, the default of most SDKs, or http://<tram>:4318 with OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf Instrumented applications; no agent to run Sidecar An agent in the application's pod scrapes or reads it and sends OTLP to TRAM Per-application settings, or isolation between tenants; costs resources in every pod Node agent An agent per node, e.g. a DaemonSet, reads the logs of all pods on the node and scrapes their metrics The usual way for logs and scraped metrics on Kubernetes Gateway A central agent scrapes many targets, or receives protocols TRAM does not speak, and forwards to TRAM Few targets, or protocols other than OTLP Broker Producers publish OTLP protobuf messages to NATS, Kafka or AMQP; a Broker Source reads them Decoupling senders from TRAM, or replaying data

Agents send OTLP over gRPC to the source's grpc_port, or over HTTP, protobuf or JSON, to its http_port; both may be gzip-compressed. With the OpenTelemetry Collector, that is the otlp exporter for gRPC or the otlphttp exporter for HTTP, e.g. for scraped metrics:

receivers:
  prometheus:
    config:
      scrape_configs:
        - job_name: my-app
          static_configs:
            - targets: ["my-app:9090"]
exporters:
  otlp:
    endpoint: tram:4317          # the source's grpc_port
    tls:
      insecure: true             # the OTLP source serves gRPC without TLS
service:
  pipelines:
    metrics:
      receivers: [prometheus]
      exporters: [otlp]

TRAM answers 503, or Unavailable over gRPC, when a delivery fails or takes too long, and agents and SDKs retry it; keep their retries and queues enabled, since TRAM's delivery is at-least-once only as far as the sender retries.

items.title: One Ingress per Tenant
items.text:
When tenants send their own data, a proxy in front of TRAM can name the tenant, so the client cannot choose it: e.g. an ingress per tenant at <router-id>.example.com sets the header X-Tram-Router, and the OTLP source copies it into a resource attribute with header_attributes. Every resource of a request then carries it, and a broker sink routes each record by it, also when a batch stage has merged the requests of several tenants:

flowchart LR
    a(["Tenant A"]) -- "a.example.com" --> ia["Ingress, sets<br/>X-Tram-Router: a"]
    b(["Tenant B"]) -- "b.example.com" --> ib["Ingress, sets<br/>X-Tram-Router: b"]
    ia --> src
    ib --> src
    subgraph stream["one stream"]
        src(["OTLP source<br/>header_attributes"]) --> batch[batch] --> sink(["broker sink<br/>router. + tram.router.id + .logs"])
    end
    sink --> ra[("router.a.logs")]
    sink --> rb[("router.b.logs")]

The header decides the attribute: a value a client sends in the attribute itself is replaced or removed. See the OTLP Source for the rules, and examples/config/otlp_tenant_routing.json for a stream that validates the router ID before the batch. Let only the proxy reach the source's port, and authenticate tenants there.

items.title: Pipeline Structure
items.text:
Streams follow a tree structure with these rules:

  1. Each pipeline has exactly one source (root)
  2. Stages can be connected to the source or other stages
  3. Sinks must be connected to either the source or a stage
  4. All leaves must be sinks (no dangling stages)
flowchart LR
    subgraph stream["Stream"]
        source(["Source"]) --> stage["Stage"]
        stage --> sink(["Sink"])
        source --> sink
        stage --> stage
    end

items.title: Data Flow
items.text:
A stream processes events in memory and synchronously. The source hands each event to its stages and sinks and answers only once every sink has accepted it. Nothing is written to disk on the way, so a stream adds no storage and little latency:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as OTLP source
    participant F as filter stage
    participant K1 as OTLP sink
    participant K2 as debug sink
    C->>S: Export request
    par to every branch
        S->>F: event
        F->>K1: event
        K1-->>F: accepted by the backend
        F-->>S: done
    and
        S->>K2: event
        K2-->>S: done
    end
    S-->>C: 200 OK
    Note over C,K2: If a sink fails, or the delivery takes longer than the source's delivery_timeout,<br/>the client gets 503 and sends the data again (at-least-once).

Until the source has answered, an event exists only in memory. If the process stops, a client that retries, as OTLP exporters do, sends the events in flight again, since it got no answer. To answer clients before the destination has the data, e.g. to ride out an outage of the destination, write events ahead to disk with two streams and a buffer between them; see Buffers.

items.title: Available Components
items.text:
Type Components Sources broker, buffer, generator, otlp Stages batch, decryption, delay, encryption, filter, noop, transform, validation, value_map Sinks broker, buffer, debug, otlp

For detailed documentation on each component and its configuration, see COMPONENTS.md.

flowchart LR
    otlp_src(["otlp source<br>OTLP/HTTP, OTLP/gRPC"]) --> tram(["TRAM"])
    broker_src(["broker source"]) --> tram
    generator(["generator source"]) --> tram
    tram --> otlp_sink(["otlp sink"])
    tram --> broker_sink(["broker sink"])
    tram --> debug(["debug sink"])

items.title: Fan-out Pattern
items.text:
Route data from a single source to multiple sinks. Every sink receives every event:

curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/fanout-example \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-binary @- <<'EOF'
{
  "stream": {
    "name": "fanout-example",
    "source": {
      "name": "otlp-in",
      "type": "otlp",
      "spec": { "http_port": 4318 }
    },
    "sinks": [
      {
        "name": "console",
        "type": "debug",
        "from": "otlp-in"
      },
      {
        "name": "archive",
        "type": "broker",
        "from": "otlp-in",
        "spec": {
          "driver": "nats",
          "nats": { "url": "nats://localhost:4222" },
          "destination": {
            "logs": "'logs.' + logs.resource_logs[0].resource.attributes.get_attr('service.name')"
          }
        }
      }
    ]

EOF

The broker sink with driver: nats needs a NATS server with JetStream enabled, e.g. docker compose -f examples/nats/docker-compose.yaml up -d, and a stream for its subjects, which TRAM does not create: nats stream add telemetry --subjects 'logs.>' --defaults.

items.text:

curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/chained-pipeline \

  -d '{

      "source": {

        "type": "generator",
        "spec": { "interval": "1s" }

      "stages": [
        {

items.title: Updating a Stream
items.text:
A PUT to an existing stream changes as little as possible:

Change Effect None Nothing happens; the running stream is kept Stages, sinks or metrics only The new stages and sinks are created, events still in flight finish in the old ones, and the source switches over. The source keeps running, e.g. an OTLP source keeps its port open, and no event is lost Source The stream is stopped and created again. An OTLP source closes its port in between, so clients briefly cannot connect

If an update fails, e.g. because of an invalid component spec, the request returns an error and the previous version of the stream keeps running. Delete and create a stream to restart it completely.

If the source of a stream stops on its own, e.g. because the NATS stream of a broker source does not exist yet, TRAM restarts the stream after a delay that grows from 1 second to 1 minute while it keeps failing. A PUT of the unchanged stream restarts it right away.

Check an update before applying it with a dry run.

items.title: Stream Behavior
items.text:
• Component Type vs Name: The type field in configuration refers to the component implementation type (e.g., generator, validation), while the name field is a user-defined identifier for the component instance within a stream.
  • Connections: The from field in stages and sinks specifies which component they receive data from.
  • Tree Structure: Pipelines form a tree with the source as root, stages as intermediate nodes, and sinks as leaves.
  • Delivery Guarantee: Delivery is at-least-once, and TRAM does not deduplicate. A sink can receive the same data again, e.g. when a client retries after a 503 although some sinks had already accepted the data, when a broker message is redelivered after one branch of its stream failed, or when a publish succeeded but its acknowledgement was lost. Deduplicate at the destination where duplicates matter.

items.title: Buffers
items.text:
A stream processes events only in memory: it answers its source once every sink accepted an event, and keeps nothing on disk. A stream therefore cannot write events ahead by itself. A buffer does that with two streams: one writes events to a queue on the instance's disk with a Buffer Sink, the other reads them with a Buffer Source and delivers them. The queue name connects the two. Both streams stay synchronous and in memory; the queue between them is a broker embedded in the instance, and the Buffer Source handles deliveries like the Broker Source.

flowchart LR
    clients([OTLP clients]) --> otlp
    subgraph instance["TRAM instance"]
        subgraph writer["stream otlp-to-buffer, in memory"]
            otlp([OTLP source]) --> bufsink([buffer sink])
        end
        queue[("queue outbox<br/>in the data directory")]
        subgraph reader["stream buffer-to-otlp, in memory"]
            bufsource([buffer source]) --> batch[batch] --> otlpsink([OTLP sink])
        end
        bufsink -- "store, sync to disk" --> queue
        queue -- "deliver, retry until max_age" --> bufsource
    end
    otlpsink --> backend([destination])

This is a write-ahead log for a pipeline: the writing stream answers its clients as soon as an event is on disk, and the reading stream delivers it later, retrying while the destination is down:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant W as stream otlp-to-buffer
    participant Q as queue on disk
    participant R as stream buffer-to-otlp
    participant D as destination
    C->>W: Export request
    W->>Q: store event
    Q-->>W: synced to disk
    W-->>C: 200 OK
    Note over C,W: The client is done, the event is safe on disk.
    Q->>R: deliver event
    R->>D: send
    D-->>R: 503, destination down
    Note over Q,R: back off and retry, until max_age
    Q->>R: deliver event again
    R->>D: send
    D-->>R: 200 OK
    R-->>Q: delivered, remove event
  • The queue is local. A Buffer Source reads only the queue of its own instance. Run both streams on the same instance, on Kubernetes on the same Engine; every instance then has a queue of its own
  • Data directory. Queues live in tram server --data-dir, which has to be on a volume that outlives the process. Without it, streams with a buffer sink or source fail to build. On Kubernetes, an Engine with storage gives every instance a volume and sets it
  • One process per queue. A queue file is locked by the instance that uses it; another process cannot open it
  • Retention. The writing sink sets max_age, which the queue keeps. Deleting or suspending the reading stream discards nothing: the events wait until a reader comes back or they expire, like messages of a broker without a consumer
  • Draining a buffer. Suspend the writing stream and keep the reading one running until the queue is empty. On Kubernetes, the volumes of instances that go are drained by Jobs through the reading streams, also suspended ones; to remove an Engine's storage, suspend the writing streams first, see Removing storage
  • Throughput. Every commit is synced to disk, so the latency of the volume limits the throughput. Size the volume above max_bytes, which counts the payloads only, for the write-ahead log and space not yet returned to the file system

items.title: Suspended Streams
items.text: A stream with "suspended": true stays defined but does not run: its source is not started, and its stages and sinks are not built, so it opens no port and reads from no broker or buffer. Setting it back to false starts the stream again. Use it to pause a stream, e.g. during maintenance of a destination, or to drain a buffer.

items.title: Hold Times
items.text:
A source like OTLP waits for a delivery only for a limited time, its delivery_timeout, and then answers with 503. batch stages can hold an event back for up to their timeout, delay stages for their delay. When a stream is created or updated, TRAM adds up these hold times on the way from the source to each sink and rejects the stream if the sum reaches the source's limit: every event that does not fill its batch would be cancelled, so the stream would fail as soon as traffic gets low. The error names the stages:

stream spec is invalid: on the way to sink openobserve-traces, batch-traces (10s) can hold an event for 10s, but source otlp cancels deliveries after 8s

An update that is rejected leaves the running stream unchanged. Shorten the timeout or delay, or raise the source's delivery_timeout, and keep that below the time the clients wait. Sources without such a limit, like the Broker Source, are not checked.

items.title: Testing Streams
items.text: There are two ways to check a stream before it runs for real: test cases run its stages against sample events, locally or in CI, and a dry run asks a running instance what applying a change would do.

items.title: Test Cases
items.text:
A stream can carry test cases in tests. They are never run by loading the stream; only an explicit test run executes them:

tram test stream.json [--secrets secrets.json]

The file holds either a bare stream object or a file sync file that wraps it in {"stream": {...}}, like the examples with test cases; see otlp_with_filters.json for a stream with test cases.

flowchart LR
    inputs[/"tests[].input"/] --> testsource(["test source<br/>replaces the source"])
    subgraph tree["the stream's tree, in memory"]
        testsource --> stages["the real stages"]
        stages --> capture(["capture sinks<br/>replace the sinks"])
    end
    capture --> compare{"compare with<br/>tests[].expect"}
    compare --> result(["PASS or FAIL,<br/>exit code 0 or 1"])

The stream is loaded into its own in-memory tree: the source is replaced by a test source that emits the test inputs, and every sink by a capture sink, so no external system is contacted. The stages are the real stages and process the events.

Each test has a name, an input event and the expected outcome per sink in expect:

  • "out": <event> — sink out must receive exactly this event. Events are OTLP JSON objects with one of the keys logs, metrics or traces
  • "out": "drop" — sink out must receive nothing
  • "out": "reject" — the event must be rejected by a stage
  • a sink without an entry in expect must receive nothing
"tests": [
  {
    "name": "keeps real logs",
    "input":  {"logs": {"resourceLogs": [{"scopeLogs": [{"logRecords": [{"body": {"stringValue": "hello"}}]}]}]}},
    "expect": {"out": {"logs": {"resourceLogs": [{"scopeLogs": [{"logRecords": [{"body": {"stringValue": "hello"}}]}]}]}}}
  },
  {
    "name": "drops noise",
    "input":  {"logs": {"resourceLogs": [{"scopeLogs": [{"logRecords": [{"body": {"stringValue": "noise"}}]}]}]}},
    "expect": {"out": "drop"}
  }
]

--secrets reads a JSON file mapping "<name>/<key>" to values and resolves secretKeyRef references in stage specs. A reference that cannot be resolved is an error naming the reference, never its value. Source and sink specs are not used by a test run. The exit code is 0 when all tests pass and 1 otherwise.

items.title: Running Tests in CI
items.text:
tram test takes one file and exits with 1 if a test fails, so a CI job runs it for every stream file, e.g. with the container image, whose entry point is tram:

for f in streams/*.json; do
  docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" ghcr.io/go-tram/tram:latest test "/work/$f" || exit 1
done

Test cases are part of the stream files of the API and file sync. The Stream resource of the Kubernetes operator has no tests field, so keep the tests of a stream that runs on Kubernetes in a stream file next to its resource, and test that file.

items.title: Dry Run
items.text:
PUT /v1/streams/{name} with "dry_run": true in the request body validates the stream and reports what applying it would do, without changing the running stream. The flag is a field of the request body, not a query parameter, because the PUT body maps to the whole request message. The response holds a plan:

{
  "stream": { "...": "the requested stream" },
  "plan": {
    "action": "STREAM_PLAN_ACTION_HOT_SWAP",
    "sourceReplaced": false,
    "createdNodes": ["enrich"],
    "stoppedNodes": ["old-sink"]
  }
}

action is STREAM_PLAN_ACTION_NOOP (nothing would change), STREAM_PLAN_ACTION_HOT_SWAP (the source keeps running and its stages and sinks are replaced below it) or STREAM_PLAN_ACTION_REBUILD (the stream is new, stopped, or its source changed: it would be stopped and created again). An invalid spec is rejected with 400 as usual; nothing is applied either way.

items.title: Benchmarks
items.text:
This page shows what TRAM's pipelines and components cost, to help with sizing deployments and choosing configurations. The tables are generated by tools/benchreport from the benchmarks in the repository; see Regenerating.

Absolute numbers depend on the machine, its load and the network to NATS, so treat them as an indication for the environment below. Costs per record and the ratios between configurations carry over much better than throughput figures.

items.title: How to Read the Numbers
items.text:
• Record: a log record, metric data point or span. Event: one OTLP request or one broker message, carrying one or more records.
  • CPU per record: CPU time (user and system) of the whole process, divided by the records processed. It includes garbage collection. For the OTLP scenarios it also includes the HTTP client that generates the load in the same process, so it is an upper bound. NATS runs in a container, and its CPU time is not included.
  • Small events overstate CPU. With 1 record per event, the process mostly waits for HTTP and NATS round trips, and the Go runtime uses CPU between those short requests as well. These rows therefore show far more CPU per record than the work itself costs (compare the per-event costs under Where the Time Goes). Use the rows with 100 or 1,000 records for sizing; treat single-record rows as a pessimistic bound
  • Records/s per core: how many records one fully used CPU core can process, derived from the CPU per record. This is the figure for sizing, as TRAM is stateless and scales horizontally.
  • Records/s: the throughput actually measured on this machine. It is also limited by the number of callers and by NATS.
  • Latency: time from sending an OTLP request until TRAM answered it. TRAM answers once all sinks accepted the data, so it includes publishing to NATS.
  • Per record / per event (components): wall time of one caller. For components that wait, such as sinks waiting for a broker's acknowledgement or a disk sync, it includes the wait.
  • CPU per record / per event (components): CPU time of the whole process during the measurement, divided by the records or events. It is the cost to size with when TRAM, not the broker, is the limit. It includes the garbage collector, which runs on other cores, so it can exceed the wall time; it excludes the brokers in their containers.
  • Spread: range of the runs relative to the median. Values above 10% are flagged with ⚠️ and are less reliable.

  • NATS server: all pods publish to the same JetStream streams. A stream is written by one NATS node, so at very high load NATS, not TRAM, becomes the limit; spread the data over several streams

items.title: Streams per Instance
items.text:
The cost of processing data is shared by the replicas, but the cost of a stream itself is not: every replica that runs a stream holds its connections, goroutines and memory, and its broker sources keep asking the NATS server for messages even when there are none. This section measures that cost, so you can tell when to shard streams over several deployments with --watch-namespace or --engine (see the operator documentation) instead of running every stream on every replica.

BenchmarkStreams builds 10, 100 and 1,000 streams of one shape in one TRAM core and observes them for 10 seconds without data. Values are per stream, measured against the process before the streams were built:

  • Build: time to create the stream through the core, including connecting to NATS
  • Heap: live heap after a garbage collection. RSS is higher; see Sizing
  • NATS connections: client connections the NATS server sees. Every broker source and sink has its own
  • NATS messages/s, idle: messages the NATS server receives from the idle stream, mostly the pull requests of the broker source, which renews its request every 5 seconds
  • Idle CPU: CPU the process uses for the idle stream, as a share of one core

Idle CPU is shown for 1,000 streams only; for fewer streams it is below the noise of the process.
